PatternBloom: Empowering Agentic RAG with Externalized RL-Distilled Graph Patterns

Yi Ge Affiliation: Department of Computer Science, University of Maryland, College Park    Heng Huang Affiliation: {yige, heng}@umd.edu
Abstract

Reinforcement-learning-trained agents for retrieval-augmented generation retrieve content (passages, knowledge-graph fragments, or hyperedges) and supervise training with outcome rewards on the final answer. Across these paradigms the reasoning route through retrieved content never leaves the language model’s hidden state, conflating declarative knowledge with the procedural knowledge that recurs across queries of the same logical type; content-only methods consequently plateau as reasoning depth grows. We introduce PatternBloom, an agentic RAG framework that shifts the unit of retrieval from content (what to read) to logic (how to reason). A first RL stage scores the agent’s constructed evidence graph by a frozen oracle’s information gain through the Information-Density Reward (IDR), a size-normalized mutual-information surrogate. High-reward trajectories are distilled into a Graph Pattern Memory (GPM) of type-abstracted reasoning skeletons, and a second RL stage uses the Pattern-Augmented Reward (PAR) to couple policy to memory, turning procedural reasoning into a learnable, externalized structural prior. A 7B PatternBloom outperforms 2727 baselines by +15.0+15.0 Avg-OOD EM, with the gain compounding with reasoning depth precisely because procedural knowledge, once distilled, is reused rather than re-derived at every query. We release our code at https://github.com/EllenYiGe/PatternBloom.

1 Introduction

Retrieval-augmented language model agents must compose retrieved evidence to answer multi-hop questions over large corpora [1, 2, 3, 4]. Recent agentic systems trained with reinforcement learning (Search-R1 [5], Graph-R1 [6], R1-Searcher [7]) push this further by letting an agent decide when and what to retrieve, optimizing tool-use policies with outcome rewards [8, 9]. Across these architectures, however, supervision touches only the retrieved units and the final answer string. Rewards score the correctness of the answer, but the reasoning trajectory between query and answer (which entities the agent binds, in which order, along which logical path) is left to a black-box policy: the agent learns to read better evidence over time, yet does not learn to traverse evidence better.

Existing RAG paradigms differ primarily in what is retrieved: paragraph-based methods (Search-R1, FrugalRAG [10], R1-Searcher) return chunk-level passages; knowledge-graph methods (GraphRAG [11], HippoRAG [12, 13], LinearRAG [14], LightRAG [15], GFM-RAG [16]) build entity-relation graphs offline and return subgraphs; and structure-aware methods (StructRAG [17], Graph-R1, Structure-R1 [18]) retrieve task-adaptive units such as hyperedges or summarized clusters. Despite these different retrieval units, the three paradigms share a common limitation: the reasoning route through the retrieved evidence never leaves the language model’s hidden state. Paragraph methods leave entity binding and relation inference to opaque attention; knowledge-graph and structure-aware methods expose entities as graph nodes, but the path through those nodes that solves a given query is still inferred at run time. Figure 1 (left) frames this collectively as content retrieval: the agent decides what to read (a passage, a subgraph, or a hyperedge), but the reasoning skeleton that links those units is never itself retrieved. The cost compounds on compositionally complex queries, motivating a retrieval target that is the reasoning route itself.

Why richer content does not solve the problem.

The plateau on deeper queries is not primarily a retrieval-recall failure: knowledge-graph and structure-aware methods often achieve high entity-level coverage. The bottleneck is procedural. Two queries about different films, “in which country was the director of Black Gold born?” and “where was the director of Top Gun from?”, share an identical logical structure yet are solved from scratch each time: their typed reasoning skeleton, from film to person to country, is encoded only in the policy’s hidden activations and discarded when the episode ends. Cognitively, this conflates declarative knowledge (the facts to retrieve) with procedural knowledge (the operations that recur across queries of the same logical type) [19]. The two memory systems are functionally distinct in human reasoning and require different storage and retrieval mechanisms; a retrieval system that augments only declarative memory will, by construction, fail to compound experience across queries that share the same procedural skeleton.

From content retrieval to logic retrieval.

To this end, we introduce PatternBloom, an agentic RAG system that shifts the retrieval target from content (what to read) to logic (how to reason). The unit of retrieval is a graph pattern (Fig. 1, right): a small directed skeleton over typed entity slots that prescribes how to traverse retrieved evidence rather than what evidence to read. The skeleton is type-abstracted, so the same pattern serves any query of the same logical structure (concrete examples in §3.3), making procedural knowledge an explicit, retrievable object rather than a behavior latent in policy weights. A two-stage RL pipeline trains and exploits this externalized memory. Stage I uses an Information-Density Reward to supervise the agent on the information content of the constructed evidence graph rather than on the answer string, promoting the graph to a directly supervised quantity. An inter-stage distillation extracts type-abstracted skeletons from high-reward trajectories into a Graph Pattern Memory. Stage II uses a Pattern-Augmented Reward to couple the policy to the frozen memory, crediting trajectories that traverse retrieved patterns and turning procedural reasoning from a soft prompt hint into a gradient signal. Where prior systems retrieve passages (paragraph methods), subgraphs (knowledge-graph methods), or hyperedges (structure-aware methods), PatternBloom retrieves a typed reasoning skeleton: the logic itself.

Realizing this paradigm shift surfaces three concrete challenges: (C1) supervising the constructed evidence graph as an information object rather than scoring only the answer string; (C2) externalizing reasoning patterns in a form that is reusable across queries and backbones; and (C3) coupling a frozen pattern store back to the policy as a process-level gradient signal. Our main contributions, summarized below, address (C1)–(C3) respectively via the Information-Density Reward, the Graph Pattern Memory, and the Pattern-Augmented Reward.

  • •

    A new retrieval paradigm for agentic RAG: from content to logic. PatternBloom reframes agentic RAG by retrieving typed reasoning skeletons rather than content units. Stored in an externalized Graph Pattern Memory (GPM) auto-distilled from a Stage-I RL agent’s own high-reward trajectories, these skeletons make procedural knowledge a first-class retrievable artefact: inspectable, frozen at deployment, and reusable across queries and backbones.

  • •

    An information-theoretic two-stage RL framework. Stage I supervises the constructed evidence graph itself via the Information-Density Reward (IDR); Theorem 1 establishes IDR as a bounded monotone surrogate for size-normalized conditional mutual information, the first information-theoretic reward design for agentic graph construction. Stage II couples the policy to the frozen GPM via the Pattern-Augmented Reward (PAR), promoting pattern coverage from a soft prompt hint to a process-level gradient signal.

  • •

    Procedural-knowledge accumulation as a new scaling axis. A 7B PatternBloom outperforms 2727 baselines by +15.0+15.0 Avg-OOD EM; the gain compounds with reasoning depth where content-only retrieval saturates, and the same frozen pattern memory transfers across backbone families (1.51.5B–3232B), establishing pattern retrieval as a scaling axis distinct from larger backbones, deeper retrieval, or richer prompts.

2 Related Work

Structured retrieval-augmented generation.

Retrieval-augmented generation [1, 20, 21, 22, 23] has progressively moved toward structured evidence. Knowledge-graph methods build offline graphs and return subgraphs (GraphRAG [11], HippoRAG [12, 13], LightRAG [15], LinearRAG [14], GFM-RAG [16]); hypergraph variants extend to nn-ary facts (HyperGraphRAG [24], Graph-R1 [6]); adaptive-structure methods select per-query formats (StructRAG [17], Structure-R1 [18]). Across this line the structure is fixed at retrieval time, and the agent receives content fragments rather than a reasoning path.

Reinforcement learning for agentic RAG.

A complementary line trains agents end-to-end with policy gradients [25, 26, 8, 9]: Search-R1 [5], R1-Searcher [7], FrugalRAG [10], Graph-R1, Structure-R1, and ReSearch [27] share answer-level outcome rewards; prompted variants couple iterative retrieval with chain-of-thought [28, 29, 30, 31, 32].

Two constraints bottleneck both lines: (i) supervision is surface-form, scoring the answer string but never the evidence graph as an information object; (ii) the retrieval unit is content tied to specific entities, not the procedural skeleton that recurs across queries of the same logical type. PatternBloom addresses both via an information-theoretic graph reward and an externalized Graph Pattern Memory of type-abstracted skeletons; a method-by-method comparison appears in Appendix J.

3 PatternBloom: Logic-Enhanced RL with Externalized Graph Pattern Memory

Section 2 identified two constraints that bottleneck prior agentic RAG: surface-form supervision that never interrogates the constructed evidence graph, and a content-only retrieval target that leaves procedural reasoning latent in policy weights. PatternBloom is built around one principle that addresses both: supervise the agent on what evidence it gathers and how it traverses that evidence, with each component an externalized, learnable object rather than a behavior to be hoped for. Stage I (§3.2) targets the first constraint via the Information-Density Reward (IDR), which scores the evidence graph’s information content under a frozen oracle and so promotes the graph itself to a directly supervised quantity. Trajectories from the Stage-I best checkpoint are distilled (§3.3) into a Graph Pattern Memory (GPM) of type-abstracted reasoning skeletons; Stage II (§3.4) couples the frozen GPM to the policy via the Pattern-Augmented Reward (PAR), turning procedural reasoning into a retrievable, learnable structural prior and addressing the second constraint. Figure 2 shows the pipeline; Algorithm 1 (Appendix A) gives the formal procedure.

3.1 Preliminaries

We consider multi-hop QA over a corpus 𝒞\mathcal{C} of Wikipedia chunks, with dataset 𝒟={(qi,ai∗)}\mathcal{D}=\{(q_{i},a^{*}_{i})\} where each query qq requires reasoning over two or more retrieved facts. We pre-build a hypergraph index H=(V,Ehyper,Xtext)H=(V,E_{\text{hyper}},X_{\text{text}}) over 𝒞\mathcal{C} following Gutiérrez et al. [12], Luo et al. [6]: entity nodes VV are connected by hyperedges EhyperE_{\text{hyper}} that group facts from each chunk, and chunk text XtextX_{\text{text}} is preserved for retrieval (Appendix G.2). nn-ary hyperedges preserve the intra-chunk co-occurrence that binary triples discard, exposing the typed neighborhoods that pattern abstraction (§3.3) will exploit. The agent policy πθ\pi_{\theta} is a tool-use language model that interleaves ⟨think⟩\langle\textsf{think}\rangle, ⟨query⟩\langle\textsf{query}\rangle, ⟨graph⟩\langle\textsf{graph}\rangle, ⟨answer⟩\langle\textsf{answer}\rangle blocks, accumulating an evidence graph 𝒢⊆H\mathcal{G}\subseteq H over multiple turns. The oracle 𝒪\mathcal{O} (Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct [33]) is held frozen and used only at training time to score evidence-graph quality via logP𝒪(⋅∣q,⋅)\log P_{\mathcal{O}}(\cdot\mid q,\cdot): a frozen scorer keeps the reward landscape stationary across both stages and rules out reward-gaming that an online critic invites. The pattern memory ℳ\mathcal{M} is defined precisely in §3.3.

Per-stage GRPO objective.

PatternBloom’s two rewards target complementary failure modes: RIDRR_{\textsc{IDR}} (Stage I) addresses what the policy fails to gather, and RPARR_{\textsc{PAR}} (Stage II) addresses how the policy fails to structure its reasoning. We instantiate both stages with GRPO [9]—group-relative advantages remove the value-function critic, which becomes high-variance under the sparse trajectory-level rewards typical of long tool-use rollouts—through a single policy-gradient template with RR supplying the per-stage signal:

ℒPatternBloom​(θ,R)=𝔼q,{τi}​[1G​∑imin⁡(ri​(θ)​A^i,clip⁡(ri​(θ),1−ϵ,1+ϵ)​A^i)]−βDKL[πθ∥πref],\begin{split}\mathcal{L}_{\text{PatternBloom}}(\theta;\,R)={}&\mathbb{E}_{q,\{\tau_{i}\}}\!\Bigl[\tfrac{1}{G}\textstyle\sum_{i}\min\bigl(r_{i}(\theta)\,\hat{A}_{i},\,\mathrm{clip}(r_{i}(\theta),1{-}\epsilon,1{+}\epsilon)\,\hat{A}_{i}\bigr)\Bigr]\\ &-\beta\,D_{\mathrm{KL}}\bigl[\pi_{\theta}\,\|\,\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}\bigr],\end{split} (1)

where A^i=(R⁡(τi)−meanG​R)/(stdG​R+δ)\hat{A}_{i}=\bigl(R(\tau_{i})-\mathrm{mean}_{G}R\bigr)/\bigl(\mathrm{std}_{G}R+\delta\bigr) is the within-group standardized advantage, ri​(θ)r_{i}(\theta) is the per-rollout importance ratio, and πref\pi_{\mathrm{ref}} is reset between stages (the SFT backbone for Stage I, the Stage-I best policy for Stage II) so each stage is anchored to the previous stage’s gains. Both rewards are bounded in [−1,1][-1,1] via a binary format gate. Stage I sets R=RIDRR=R_{\textsc{IDR}} (Eq. 3); Stage II sets R=RPARR=R_{\textsc{PAR}} (Eq. 6); hyperparameters are listed in Appendix G.16.

3.2 Stage I: Evidence Construction with the Information-Density Reward

Existing RL-RAG agents supervise training with answer-level signals on the predicted string [5, 7] or entity-presence checks on the constructed graph [6]. None interrogate the graph’s information content as a whole: a 2020-triple noisy graph and a 33-triple clean one receive the same reward provided both yield a matching answer. This blindness leaves πθ\pi_{\theta} with no signal to prefer minimum-sufficient evidence over verbose-but-correct rollouts, and the gap widens with reasoning depth (Appendix G.10). IDR closes this gap by promoting the constructed graph itself to the supervised quantity.

Let ser⁡(𝒢)\mathrm{ser}(\mathcal{G}) serialize the evidence graph as a sequence of typed triples. The information gain of 𝒢\mathcal{G} relative to the empty graph is

Δ​log⁡p⁡(𝒢)≔log⁡P𝒪​(a∗∣q,ser⁡(𝒢))−log⁡P𝒪​(a∗∣q,∅),\Delta\log p(\mathcal{G})\coloneqq\log P_{\mathcal{O}}\bigl(a^{*}\mid q,\mathrm{ser}(\mathcal{G})\bigr)-\log P_{\mathcal{O}}\bigl(a^{*}\mid q,\emptyset\bigr), (2)

which equals the conditional pointwise mutual information PMI⁡(𝒢;a∗∣q)\mathrm{PMI}(\mathcal{G};a^{*}\mid q) between graph and answer given the query (cf. Eq. 9). The Information-Density Reward wraps the per-triple-normalized gain in a sigmoid, gates by the format reward RfmtR_{\text{fmt}} so malformed trajectories collapse to −1-1, and rewards trajectories that achieve high information density:

RIDR(τ)=−1+Rfmt(τ)+𝟙{Rfmt=1}⋅σ(Δ​log⁡p​(𝒢)max⁡(|𝒢|,1)⋅T),R_{\textsc{IDR}}(\tau)=-1+R_{\text{fmt}}(\tau)+\mathds{1}\{R_{\text{fmt}}=1\}\cdot\sigma\!\left(\frac{\Delta\log p(\mathcal{G})}{\max(|\mathcal{G}|,1)\cdot T}\right), (3)

with temperature T=1T=1. Three design choices in Eq. 3 are deliberate. (i) Size normalization. Dividing by |𝒢||\mathcal{G}| favors short anchor-to-answer paths: low-information triples grow |𝒢||\mathcal{G}| faster than Δ​log⁡p\Delta\log p, so verbose-but-correct rollouts strictly lose to minimum-sufficient ones, closing a loophole that entity-presence rewards leave open [6]. (ii) Sigmoid wrapping. The sigmoid bounds the reward in [0,1][0,1] so within-group GRPO advantages remain well-scaled across queries whose absolute Δ​log⁡p\Delta\log p scale varies by orders of magnitude. (iii) Format gating. The RfmtR_{\text{fmt}} multiplier collapses malformed trajectories to −1-1, so any density improvement is conditional on a well-formed graph and the policy cannot trade structural validity for content. Theorem 1 (Appendix E) shows that maximizing RIDRR_{\textsc{IDR}} via GRPO is consistent with maximizing the size-normalized conditional mutual information I⁡(𝒢;a∗∣q)/(|𝒢|⋅T)I(\mathcal{G};a^{*}\mid q)/(|\mathcal{G}|\cdot T), with the divisive normalizer realizing an adaptive Information-Bottleneck multiplier [34, 35] βeff=1/(|𝒢|⋅T)\beta_{\text{eff}}=1/(|\mathcal{G}|\cdot T). IDR thereby provides the first information-theoretic reward design for agentic graph construction, replacing the surface-form heuristics that bottleneck prior work with a principled signal that scores the graph as a whole.

3.3 Pattern Distillation: Building the Externalized Procedural Memory

A retrieved triple like (Black Gold,directed_by,Leslie Martinson)(\textsc{Black Gold},\texttt{directed\_by},\textsc{Leslie Martinson}) is query-specific and never recurs, but many queries share the same logical structure: “given a film, find the director’s nationality” applies across thousands of film–director–country instances. The procedural component of multi-hop reasoning—how types of facts compose—recurs while the instances change, yet prior systems leave this regularity implicit in policy weights (§2). PatternBloom lifts each instance triple to a type-abstracted skeleton (film,directed_by,person),(person,born_in,country)(\textsc{film},\texttt{directed\_by},\textsc{person}),(\textsc{person},\texttt{born\_in},\textsc{country}) that is reusable across all instances of the same query type, and stores these skeletons in an external memory auto-distilled from the policy’s own high-reward Stage-I trajectories. Three properties follow from this construction: type abstraction makes each entry an equivalence class over instances and so amortizes the cost of one query’s reasoning across thousands of structurally similar ones; externalization makes the memory inspectable, freezable, and reusable across backbones; and self-distillation keeps the memory aligned with what this policy actually solves, rather than a hand-curated wishlist.

Graph pattern.

A graph pattern PP is a tuple (σ,skel,desc,n)(\sigma,\mathrm{skel},\mathrm{desc},n) where σ∈𝒮\sigma\in\mathcal{S} is a query signature, skel\mathrm{skel} is a connected directed graph of typed entity nodes (the reasoning skeleton), desc\mathrm{desc} is a short natural-language descriptor, and nn is a usage count. The Graph Pattern Memory ℳ\mathcal{M} is the learned external store

ℳ={(σi,skeli,desci,ni)}i=1|ℳ|,\mathcal{M}=\bigl\{\bigl(\sigma_{i},\,\mathrm{skel}_{i},\,\mathrm{desc}_{i},\,n_{i}\bigr)\bigr\}_{i=1}^{|\mathcal{M}|}, (4)

populated by distilling Stage-I trajectories. Signatures are extracted by a deterministic parser (e.g., lookup(country)[FILM]); entity types in the skeleton come from the type-abstraction step, and descriptors are auto-generated from the signature and a representative answer instance.

Coverage and retrieval.

At Stage II, patterns are retrieved by encoding σ⁡(q)\sigma(q) with a sentence encoder and ranking ℳ\mathcal{M} by cosine similarity in a FAISS [36] index. The trajectory–pattern coverage

𝒞⁡(τ,P)=|abs(τ)∩P.skel||P.skel|,abs⁡(τ)≔{(type⁡(h),r,type⁡(t)):(h,r,t)∈τ},\mathcal{C}(\tau,P)=\frac{|\,\mathrm{abs}(\tau)\cap P.\mathrm{skel}\,|}{|P.\mathrm{skel}|},\quad\mathrm{abs}(\tau)\coloneqq\{(\mathrm{type}(h),r,\mathrm{type}(t)):(h,r,t)\in\tau\}, (5)

divides by the skeleton size rather than by the union, so a trajectory that contains the required reasoning steps plus exploratory extras receives full credit. We use the top-11 match Pq∗∈ℳP^{*}_{q}\in\mathcal{M} as the coverage signal in RPARR_{\textsc{PAR}} and feed the top-33 retrieved patterns to the agent’s prompt as a ⟨knowledge⟩\langle\textsf{knowledge}\rangle hint, allowing the policy to compare alternative skeletons before committing to a trajectory.

Memory construction.

The memory ℳ0\mathcal{M}_{0} is built between Stage I and Stage II from high-IDR trajectories (RIDR≥0.85R_{\textsc{IDR}}\geq 0.85, the empirical top-quartile threshold; Appendix C); two patterns merge when their signature embeddings have cosine similarity ≥θmerge=0.85\geq\theta_{\mathrm{merge}}=0.85. We freeze ℳ0\mathcal{M}_{0} throughout Stage II and at inference: a non-stationary memory chasing a non-stationary policy invites collapse, while a frozen memory yields a stationary reward signal during refinement and a deterministic retrieval store at deployment. The same frozen 2727-skeleton memory (Tab. 16) then transfers across distribution shift, a test query walks a skeleton distilled purely from training (Fig. 4), evidencing that procedural knowledge, once externalized, generalizes beyond its training distribution.

3.4 Stage II: Policy Refinement with the Pattern-Augmented Reward

Feeding retrieved patterns to the policy’s prompt provides only a soft prior, with no gradient signal pushing the trajectory to align with the retrieved skeleton: the policy is free to ignore the hint and revert to whatever idiosyncratic chain it has already learned, especially when answer-level reward is uninformative. PatternBloom promotes pattern coverage from a soft prior to a process-level reward by combining answer-level F1F_{1} with the trajectory–pattern coverage of Eq. 5:

RPAR(τ)=−1+Rfmt(τ)+𝟙{Rfmt=1}⋅[(1−λP)F1(a^,a∗)+λP𝒞(τ,Pq∗)].R_{\textsc{PAR}}(\tau)=-1+R_{\text{fmt}}(\tau)+\mathds{1}\{R_{\text{fmt}}=1\}\cdot\bigl[\,(1-\lambda_{P})\,F_{1}(\hat{a},a^{*})+\lambda_{P}\,\mathcal{C}(\tau,P^{*}_{q})\,\bigr]. (6)

The convex combination ensures pattern coverage acts as a structural prior that shapes how the policy reasons without overriding the answer signal that defines task success. The shaping weight λP∈[0,0.3]\lambda_{P}\in[0,0.3] keeps answer correctness dominant, in line with the bounded-potential shaping principle of Ng et al. [37], which guarantees policy invariance under shaping rewards small relative to the task reward. We select λP=0.2\lambda_{P}=0.2 as the default through a sweep over {0,0.1,0.2,0.5}\{0,0.1,0.2,0.5\} on a held-out 1k-query slice (Appendix D); values above 0.30.3 destabilize the IDR-learned graph-construction behavior because pattern coverage begins to dominate the answer-level signal, and we therefore impose this empirical bound. Setting λP=0\lambda_{P}=0 recovers a pure F1F_{1} reward. PatternBloom warm-starts πθ\pi_{\theta} from πθ1∗\pi_{\theta^{*}_{1}} and continues maximizing ℒPatternBloom​(θ,RPAR)\mathcal{L}_{\text{PatternBloom}}(\theta;R_{\textsc{PAR}}) (Eq. 1); at deployment, πθ2∗\pi_{\theta^{*}_{2}} and the frozen ℳ0\mathcal{M}_{0} operate over the same hypergraph HH (Appendix G.3). Together, IDR and PAR realize the paradigm shift of §1: both the constructed evidence graph and the retrieved reasoning skeleton become supervisable, externalized objects rather than behaviors latent in policy weights, and the gain compounds with reasoning depth precisely because procedural knowledge, once distilled, is reused rather than re-derived at every query.

4 Experiments

4.1 Experimental Setup

Datasets.

Seven QA benchmarks split as in-distribution (HotpotQA [2], 2WikiMultiHopQA [3]; 1414K FlashRAG training queries, seed 4242) and out-of-distribution (MuSiQue [4], NQ [38], TriviaQA [39], PopQA [40], Bamboogle [41]). We sample 1,0001{,}000 test instances per dataset (seed 4040); Bamboogle uses its full 125125 items. The 55-of-77 OOD majority is strictly harder than the IID-only protocol of Graph-R1 [6].

Baselines.

2727 baselines span four families: training-free RAG on GPT-4o-mini (HippoRAG 2 [13], GraphRAG [11], LightRAG [15], StructRAG [17], LinearRAG [14], GFM-RAG [16], HyperGraphRAG [24]); RL-trained chunk retrieval (Search-R1 [5], R1-Searcher [7], FrugalRAG [10]); RL-trained graph retrieval (Graph-R1 [6], Structure-R1 [18]); plus prompt-engineered (7272B) and large-scale (1414B–≥30\geq 30B) reference panels (Tab. 1). RL methods share identical training data and seeds; PatternBloom occupies a previously unfilled cell: a trained agent over a graph substrate with procedural memory.

Metrics, backbones, compute.

We report answer correctness (EM, F1, Contain-Acc), retrieval quality (R@5, Evidence Recall), pattern faithfulness (RPF, P-Cov; §4.4), efficiency, and human + LLM-judge scores. Backbones: Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct [33] (primary), Qwen3-8B-Instruct [42] (cross-backbone), four Qwen2.5 sizes (1.51.5B/77B/1414B/3232B) for scaling. Full settings and metric definitions: Appendix G.16, 6.

4.2 Main Results

PatternBloom (Q2.5-7B) is rank-11 on EM and F1 across all seven datasets in Tab. 1, leading R1-Searcher by 15.015.0 Avg-OOD EM and the 7272B prompt-engineered RAG panel by 17.117.1 Avg-OOD EM at one-tenth the parameter count. The same frozen GPM transfers to a Qwen3-8B backbone, where PatternBloom leads every 88B entry on Avg-OOD by 11.311.3 EM, indicating the gain originates in the procedural-memory mechanism rather than backbone-specific tuning. The IID-to-OOD gap stays under 1.51.5 EM on either backbone (against 4.14.1 and 3.33.3 EM for Search-R1 and Graph-R1), and PatternBloom is rank-11 on every Avg-OOD metric (EM, F1, Contain-Acc, R@5, Evidence Recall), so the gain transfers across the five out-of-distribution test sets without overfitting to the IID training corpus.

4.3 Component Analysis

The three components are jointly necessary. Removing PAR drops F1 from 55.955.9 to 44.144.1, a larger loss than disabling GPM (46.646.6) or skipping IDR (52.952.9): PAR is the only mechanism supplying a process-level gradient signal, GPM the structural prior it exploits, and IDR’s standalone effect is partially recovered by Stage II. The pattern-coverage weight is concave around λP=0.2\lambda_{P}=0.2 (55.955.9 F1; λP∈{0,0.1,0.5}\lambda_{P}\in\{0,0.1,0.5\} each lose 1010–1313 F1), confirming the bound λP≤0.3\lambda_{P}\leq 0.3 derived in §3.4 from Ng et al. [37]. Memory access is all-or-nothing: top-11/55/1010 retrieval cluster around 4343 F1 while the full |ℳ|=27|\mathcal{M}|=27 pool jumps to 55.955.9 F1, so the gain comes from the pool’s joint coverage rather than any single dominant skeleton.

4.4 Reasoning Quality

We complement answer-level scores with two pattern-quality signals introduced in this work: RPF (Reasoning Path Faithfulness, fraction of trajectory turns invoking ≥1\geq 1 stored pattern) and P-Cov (Pattern Coverage, fraction of trajectories whose retrieved pattern matches the oracle-best signature). Both drop monotonically as PatternBloom components are removed and reach zero with GPM disabled (by construction); P-Cov correlates with answer EM (ρ=0.87\rho=0.87 across the four PatternBloom variants), evidence that pattern coverage is a faithful surrogate for reasoning quality rather than a separate dimension.

4.5 Multi-Size Scaling and Cross-Backbone Transfer

PatternBloom retrains at four Qwen2.5 sizes (1.51.5B/77B/1414B/3232B) and one Qwen3-8B variant (per-size scores in Tab. 1 panels (b)–(e); discussion in Appendix G.5) and ranks first on the average column at every size band. The 1.51.5B variant attains 28.428.4 Avg. EM, competitive with 77B chunk-RL baselines (Search-R1 77B at 21.621.6) at one-quarter the parameter count, while PatternBloom (Q3-8B) leads all 88B entries on Avg-OOD (43.443.4 EM), confirming cross-backbone transfer. Inference latency stays within 0.40.4 s of Graph-R1 (Appendix G.4). Fig. 3 consolidates the Pareto: PatternBloom sits on the cost-quality frontier (a) and attains the flattest depth-decay (α=−1.10\alpha=-1.10 vs. Search-R1’s −2.91-2.91, b), substantiating the architectural claim of §1: procedural memory is an additive architectural component, not a backbone-specific tuning trick.

4.6 Behavior, Failures, and Human Study

Question-type behavior.

Against Graph-R1 (the only directly comparable RL-trained graph-RAG agent), PatternBloom uses 0.40.4–0.90.9 fewer turns per query in every category (Tab. 4): typed pattern templates replace exploratory iterations with one-shot lookups. Per-category EM/F1 and hop-stratified MuSiQue: Appendix G.11, G.10.

Residual error categories.

Errors group into four categories (Appendix G.15): three generic to graph-RAG (entity disambiguation, numerical reasoning, predicate canonicalisation), and one specific to procedural memory (signature mismatch), addressed by an inference-time pattern-admission extension (§I).

Human study and case illustrations.

Fig. 3(c) reports a blind human study on 3030 random queries: PatternBloom leads on every 11–55 Likert criterion, with the largest gain +0.85+0.85 on Pattern Reusability over Structure-R1 and the highest inter-annotator agreement (α=0.74\alpha=0.74). Fig. 4 contrasts the three paradigms qualitatively: structure-based retrieval fabricates names, chunk-based retrieval substitutes the query’s subject, and PatternBloom’s typed-skeleton retrieval anchors the trajectory to retrieved structure. Trajectories and additional cases: Appendix G.8.

5 Conclusion

Multi-hop reasoning systems have so far retrieved content units (paragraphs, knowledge-graph fragments, or hyperedges), yet the primitive that compounds with reasoning depth is logic: the type-abstracted reasoning skeleton applicable across queries that share compositional structure. We realize this paradigm shift in PatternBloom, an RL framework whose Information-Density Reward provides the first information-theoretic grounding for graph-construction RL (a bounded monotone surrogate for size-normalized conditional mutual information), and whose Pattern-Augmented Reward turns a frozen Graph Pattern Memory into a learnable structural prior. The gain compounds with reasoning depth, a property absent from content-based retrieval, precisely because procedural knowledge, once externalized, accumulates across queries rather than dissolving into policy weights at each episode end; the same frozen pattern store further transfers across out-of-distribution benchmarks and backbone scales, evidencing that what is being learned is reasoning structure, not benchmark-specific content. PatternBloom thereby reframes retrieval-augmented reasoning from a content-fetching problem into one of procedural-knowledge accumulation, opening a scaling axis distinct from larger backbones, deeper retrieval, or richer prompts.

Appendix

 

Appendix A PatternBloom Training Procedure

Algorithm 1 formalizes the training procedure of PatternBloom described in §3: Stage I optimizes evidence-graph construction with the Information-Density Reward RIDRR_{\textsc{IDR}}, an offline distillation step lifts high-quality Stage-I trajectories into the frozen Graph Pattern Memory ℳ0\mathcal{M}_{0}, and Stage II refines the policy under the Pattern-Augmented Reward RPARR_{\textsc{PAR}} on top of that memory. The shared GRPO objective ℒPatternBloom​(θ,R)\mathcal{L}_{\text{PatternBloom}}(\theta;R) is defined in Eq. 1 with R∈{RIDR,RPAR}R\in\{R_{\textsc{IDR}},R_{\textsc{PAR}}\} specifying the per-stage learning signal.

At inference time the deployed agent invokes only the trained policy πθ2∗\pi_{\theta^{*}_{2}} and the retriever; the oracle is discarded after Stage I training, and the pattern memory ℳ0\mathcal{M}_{0} serves as a read-only retrieval store. The detailed inference walkthrough appears at the end of §3.4.

Appendix B IDR Implementation Details

Format-gated reward composition.

The format reward Rfmt​(τ)∈{0,1}R_{\text{fmt}}(\tau)\in\{0,1\} is binary: a trajectory τ\tau receives Rfmt=1R_{\text{fmt}}=1 iff each turn parses as the expected interleaving of ⟨think⟩\langle\textsf{think}\rangle, ⟨query⟩\langle\textsf{query}\rangle, ⟨graph⟩\langle\textsf{graph}\rangle, and (terminal turn only) ⟨answer⟩\langle\textsf{answer}\rangle blocks; otherwise Rfmt=0R_{\text{fmt}}=0. Combined with the sigmoid kernel in Eq. 3, malformed trajectories yield RIDR=−1R_{\textsc{IDR}}=-1, well-formed-but-uninformative trajectories yield −1+1+σ⁡(Δ​log⁡p/(|𝒢|​T))∈[0,1]-1+1+\sigma(\Delta\log p/(|\mathcal{G}|T))\in[0,1], and the upper bound RIDR=1R_{\textsc{IDR}}=1 is asymptotically reached as Δ​log⁡p/(|𝒢|​T)→∞\Delta\log p/(|\mathcal{G}|T)\to\infty. Hence RIDR∈[−1,1]R_{\textsc{IDR}}\in[-1,1].

Numerical safeguards.

The sigmoid argument Δ​log⁡p/(|𝒢|​T)\Delta\log p/(|\mathcal{G}|\,T) is clipped to [−50,50][-50,50] before evaluation: outside this range, σ⁡(⋅)\sigma(\cdot) is numerically indistinguishable from {0,1}\{0,1\}, and clipping eliminates a class of NaN-producing edge cases under extreme oracle log-probability gaps. Empty graphs (|𝒢|=0|\mathcal{G}|=0) are treated as information-neutral via σ⁡(0)=0.5\sigma(0)=0.5; combined with Rfmt=1R_{\text{fmt}}=1, the trajectory’s reward is −1+1+0.5=0.5-1+1+0.5=0.5, neither rewarded nor penalized for absent evidence.

Demonstration-template anti-hack.

We strip demonstration-template placeholder entities (e.g., EntityA, EntityName, NextEntity) from each ⟨graph⟩\langle\textsf{graph}\rangle block before computing |𝒢||\mathcal{G}| and serializing for the oracle. Without this filter, the policy can copy placeholder triples shown in the system prompt’s in-context examples; such copies pass Rfmt=1R_{\text{fmt}}=1 yet carry no information about qq, opening a reward-hacking pathway. The filter is purely syntactic (case-folded match against a fixed placeholder vocabulary) and introduces no learnable parameters.

Caps and caching.

Each evidence graph is capped at 1010 graph blocks per trajectory and 2020 triples per block, for a hard upper bound of |𝒢|≤200|\mathcal{G}|\leq 200 triples; this matches the agent’s interaction budget and bounds oracle context length to under the 40964096-token serialization limit. The empty-graph baseline log⁡P𝒪​(a∗∣q,∅)\log P_{\mathcal{O}}(a^{*}\mid q,\emptyset) depends only on (q,a∗)(q,a^{*}) and is cached per query during training.

Appendix C Graph Pattern Memory Implementation Details

This appendix expands the implementation of the Graph Pattern Memory GPM introduced in §3.3.

C.1 Multi-Skeleton Pattern Storage

The main paper (§3.3) describes each pattern as carrying a single skeleton. The implementation generalizes this: each pattern stores a list of distinct skeletons (typically a small handful per signature in practice), and coverage is taken as the maximum over them.

The motivation is structural diversity: two trajectories that share a query signature can produce structurally different evidence graphs that both clear the high-quality threshold RIDR≥0.85R_{\textsc{IDR}}\geq 0.85. For instance, a query with signature compare(by[birth_year])[FILM] can be answered either via a direct two-hop chain through both films’ release dates, or via a four-hop comparison that first resolves both directors and then their birth years. A single-skeleton schema would force one to overwrite the other, losing valid alternative reasoning paths for the same query type.

We therefore store path_patterns as a list of skeleton lists, each pattern carrying its accumulated set of distinct typed-triple sequences distilled from same-signature trajectories that merged at construction time. During offline merge (§C.5), an incoming skeleton not already present in the existing pattern’s skeleton list is appended; the pattern’s running averages of usage count nn, mean F1F_{1}, and mean RIDRR_{\textsc{IDR}} are updated incrementally. Coverage at PAR computation becomes

𝒞⁡(τ,P)=maxskel∈P.skel​_​list⁡|abs⁡(τ)∩skel||skel|,\mathcal{C}(\tau,P)=\max_{\mathrm{skel}\in P.\mathrm{skel\_list}}\frac{|\mathrm{abs}(\tau)\cap\mathrm{skel}|}{|\mathrm{skel}|}, (7)

i.e., the trajectory is rewarded for matching any of the pattern’s known skeletons.

C.2 Signature Dispatch

Signature dispatch is the function σ:𝒬→ℝd\sigma:\mathcal{Q}\to\mathbb{R}^{d} that turns a natural-language query qq into a vector key for cosine-similarity lookup against ℳ\mathcal{M}. Conceptually it answers a single question: which of the |ℳ||\mathcal{M}| stored skeletons is the right procedural prior for this query? The worked example below shows what σ\sigma produces on three real queries from our test sets.

Signature form.

The signature is a two-part string. The first part is an archetype keyword extracted from the query by deterministic regex matching (e.g., lookup_chain(person) for chained-lookup queries, compare(by[date]) for date-comparison queries). The keyword captures the logical action of the question (lookup, compare, count, yesno) and its primary argument slot; we recognize fourteen such archetypes plus a sentinel unknown for queries that match none. The second part is a sorted entity-type suffix [TYPE_1+TYPE_2+…] inferred from quoted strings, year tokens, and capitalised phrases in the query under the five-class taxonomy of Appendix C.3. The suffix is what lets two queries with the same archetype but different argument types (e.g., lookup_chain(person)[FILM] versus lookup_chain(person)[COUNTRY]) route to disjoint buckets.

Signature embedding.

The full signature string is encoded into a unit-norm d=1024d{=}1024-dimensional vector by the sentence encoder BGE-large-en-v1.5 [44], the same encoder used for the hyperedge dense index of Appendix G.2. Cosine similarity above θsim=0.5\theta_{\mathrm{sim}}{=}0.5 admits the nearest stored skeleton as the retrieved pattern; otherwise the cold-start fallback of Appendix D.1 fires. Because the embedding is semantic rather than purely lexical, structurally related signatures sit close in ℝd\mathbb{R}^{d}, which is what makes the third row of the worked example possible: a Bamboogle “earliest-event” query mapped to compare(by[date])[ENTITY] retrieves a skeleton distilled from a HotpotQA training trajectory under the same archetype (Table 12), even though the two queries’ surface forms differ.

C.3 Type Abstraction Taxonomy

Signature enrichment and triple typing during skeleton extraction use the deterministic five-type taxonomy (plus an EMPTY sentinel) summarized in Table 5.

The taxonomy captures the structural distinctions that matter for multi-hop reasoning (entity, year, numeric, yes/no answers) without invoking NER or external taxonomies. A fine-grained alternative that maps every entity to its closest Wikidata class via spaCy NER expands the taxonomy from 55 to roughly 3030 types and raises the type entropy of ℳ0\mathcal{M}_{0} (deterministically over the same 2727 stored patterns) from Htype=0.19H_{\mathrm{type}}=0.19 bits to Htype=1.84H_{\mathrm{type}}=1.84 bits, at the cost of an extra NER inference per query. The paper-main run uses the coarse taxonomy.

C.4 Pattern Descriptor

The descriptor field desci\mathrm{desc}_{i} in each pattern (Eq. 4) is a short human-readable string that records what the pattern resolves to on a representative anchor trajectory. We use a deterministic template:

desci=<sig>→<answer_excerpt>\mathrm{desc}_{i}=\texttt{<sig>}\;\to\;\texttt{<answer\_excerpt>}

where <sig> is the query signature (e.g., lookup(person), compare(by[birth_year])) and <answer_excerpt> is the first 8080 characters of the trajectory’s gold answer. For example, the pattern distilled from the trajectory “Who directed Black Gold (1962)?” (gold answer “Leslie H. Martinson”) has descriptor lookup(person) →\to Leslie H. Martinson. The template is intentionally simple: it makes pattern inspection and debugging trivial, and keeps the GPM construction step hyperparameter-free at the descriptor level. The coverage reward is computed on the typed skeleton (Eq. 5), not on the descriptor string, so the descriptor’s role is purely to render an inspectable representative example for each stored pattern.

C.5 Merge Threshold Sensitivity

Patterns extracted from individual high-IDR trajectories are merged offline into archetypes by clustering signature embeddings with a cosine-similarity threshold θmerge\theta_{\mathrm{merge}}. Lower thresholds produce more, finer archetypes; higher thresholds produce fewer, coarser archetypes that match a broader range of queries. Empirically, the post-distillation archetype count follows a Zipf-like distribution: the top archetype dominates with several hundred instances while the tail decays sharply.

We use θmerge=0.85\theta_{\mathrm{merge}}=0.85 throughout: this conservative threshold keeps the merged archetype count low (under-merging) but yields stable patterns whose embeddings are clustered tightly enough that the post-distillation 2727 patterns each carry several hundred high-IDR trajectories on average.

C.6 Running-Average Update on Merge

When pattern PP absorbs an incoming candidate P′P^{\prime} with cosine similarity ≥θmerge\geq\theta_{\mathrm{merge}}, the bookkeeping fields are updated by incremental running-mean

μnew=n⋅μold+xnewn+1,\mu_{\mathrm{new}}=\frac{n\cdot\mu_{\mathrm{old}}+x_{\mathrm{new}}}{n+1},

applied to count, F1¯\overline{F_{1}}, and RIDR¯\overline{R_{\textsc{IDR}}}. This makes the GPM resistant to single-trajectory outliers (a noisy high-IDR trajectory cannot single-handedly inflate a pattern’s recorded quality) while preserving order-independence: the GPM’s final state is invariant to the order in which trajectories are processed, since the running mean is associative and commutative for fixed-population merges.

C.7 FAISS Configuration

We use faiss.IndexFlatIP (flat inner-product index) with d=1024d=1024 (BGE-large-en-v1.5 embedding dimension), L2L_{2}-normalized vectors, and CPU-only execution. For the GPM sizes we observe (|ℳ|≤105|\mathcal{M}|\leq 10^{5} patterns), flat search is faster than IVF-PQ (<1<1 ms top-11 retrieval). Memory footprint is 44 MB per 1,0001{,}000 patterns (10241024 floats ×\times 44 bytes).

Appendix D Pattern-Augmented Reward Implementation Details

This appendix expands the implementation of the Pattern-Augmented Reward PAR introduced in §3.4.

D.1 Cold-Start Fallback Behavior

When the cosine similarity of σ⁡(q)\sigma(q) to the nearest GPM pattern falls below θsim=0.5\theta_{\mathrm{sim}}=0.5, we set 𝒞⁡(τ,Pq∗)=0\mathcal{C}(\tau,P^{*}_{q})=0. PAR then degenerates to

RPAR(τ)|cold=−1+Rfmt+𝟙{Rfmt=1}⋅(1−λP)⋅F1(a^,a∗),R_{\textsc{PAR}}(\tau)\big|_{\text{cold}}=-1+R_{\text{fmt}}+\mathds{1}\{R_{\text{fmt}}=1\}\cdot(1-\lambda_{P})\cdot F_{1}(\hat{a},a^{*}), (8)

i.e., 80%80\% of the F1F_{1}-only signal at the default λP=0.2\lambda_{P}=0.2, not the full F1F_{1} signal. This is by design: cold-start trajectories receive a slightly attenuated reward, providing a soft incentive for the agent to pursue queries whose signatures are well-covered by existing patterns.

The attenuated form preserves λP\lambda_{P} as a literal trade-off coefficient between answer-level and structure-level signal: the cold-start trajectory contributes only the (1−λP)(1-\lambda_{P}) fraction of the answer signal, with the remaining λP\lambda_{P} slot reserved for matched-pattern coverage.

D.2 Retrieval Threshold θsim\theta_{\mathrm{sim}}

We use θsim=0.5\theta_{\mathrm{sim}}=0.5 as the cosine-similarity floor for pattern retrieval. The choice reflects a trade-off: lower thresholds admit semantically distant patterns and inject noise into the coverage signal, while higher thresholds collapse 𝒞\mathcal{C} to 00 on legitimate matches.

D.3 Asymmetric Coverage Rationale

The asymmetry of Eq. 5 (§3.3) is quantitatively important: a symmetric Jaccard coverage 𝒞sym=|∩|/|∪|\mathcal{C}_{\mathrm{sym}}=|\cap|/|\cup| would penalize valid longer-than-skeleton trajectories at exactly the rate of one extra triple per pattern triple: at |τ|=2​|P||\tau|=2|P| even with perfect skeleton coverage we would have 𝒞sym=0.5\mathcal{C}_{\mathrm{sym}}=0.5. Our asymmetric form gives full credit (𝒞=1\mathcal{C}=1) for any superset of the skeleton, capturing the “skeleton is necessary, not maximal” semantics that matches the pattern-as-procedural-bias intent.

Appendix E Theorem 1: Proof and Information-Bottleneck Discussion

Theorem 1 (IDR as a bounded monotone surrogate for size-normalized conditional MI).

Let policy πθ\pi_{\theta} produce trajectory τ=(q,𝒢,a^)\tau=(q,\mathcal{G},\hat{a}), and let 𝒪\mathcal{O} be a frozen oracle. Define the conditional pointwise mutual information

PMI⁡(𝒢;a∗∣q)≔log⁡P𝒪​(a∗∣q,𝒢)−log⁡P𝒪​(a∗∣q),\mathrm{PMI}(\mathcal{G};a^{*}\mid q)\coloneqq\log P_{\mathcal{O}}(a^{*}\mid q,\mathcal{G})-\log P_{\mathcal{O}}(a^{*}\mid q), (9)

which satisfies 𝔼πθ​[PMI]=I⁡(𝒢;a∗∣q)\mathbb{E}_{\pi_{\theta}}[\mathrm{PMI}]=I(\mathcal{G};a^{*}\mid q). Under regularity conditions (A1)–(A4) below, the IDR kernel

J⁡(πθ)≔𝔼(q,a∗,𝒢)∼πθ​[σ⁡(PMI⁡(𝒢;a∗∣q)|𝒢|⋅T)]J(\pi_{\theta})\coloneqq\mathbb{E}_{(q,a^{*},\mathcal{G})\sim\pi_{\theta}}\!\left[\sigma\!\left(\frac{\mathrm{PMI}(\mathcal{G};a^{*}\mid q)}{|\mathcal{G}|\cdot T}\right)\right] (10)

is a bounded monotone surrogate for the size-normalized conditional mutual information I~​(πθ)≔𝔼πθ​[PMI⁡(𝒢;a∗∣q)/(|𝒢|⋅T)]\tilde{I}(\pi_{\theta})\coloneqq\mathbb{E}_{\pi_{\theta}}\!\bigl[\mathrm{PMI}(\mathcal{G};a^{*}\mid q)/(|\mathcal{G}|\cdot T)\bigr] in the following three senses:

  1. (i)

    Pointwise monotonicity. Since σ′>0\sigma^{\prime}>0 on ℝ\mathbb{R}, raising PMI/(|𝒢|⋅T)\mathrm{PMI}/(|\mathcal{G}|\cdot T) for any trajectory raises that trajectory’s contribution to JJ, so JJ tracks I~\tilde{I} trajectory-wise.

  2. (ii)

    Lipschitz gradient. Since σ′∈(0,1/4]\sigma^{\prime}\in(0,1/4], the gradient contribution of any single trajectory to JJ is bounded, providing GRPO’s group-relative advantage estimator with a stable Lipschitz signal.

  3. (iii)

    Saturation bound. On the operating regime PMI/(|𝒢|⋅T)∈ℝ≥0\mathrm{PMI}/(|\mathcal{G}|\cdot T)\in\mathbb{R}_{\geq 0} where trained policies concentrate (A4), σ\sigma is concave, so Jensen’s inequality yields J⁡(πθ)≤σ⁡(I~​(πθ))J(\pi_{\theta})\leq\sigma(\tilde{I}(\pi_{\theta})), equivalently I~​(πθ)≥log⁡J⁡(πθ)1−J⁡(πθ)\tilde{I}(\pi_{\theta})\geq\log\!\frac{J(\pi_{\theta})}{1-J(\pi_{\theta})}, characterizing the saturation regime in which JJ approaches its supremum.

This appendix provides the full proof, discusses the divisive-versus-subtractive Information-Bottleneck trade-off, and extends the result to a strict subgraph-monotonicity form. Theorem 1 grounds IDR as a tractable surrogate for size-normalized conditional mutual information: maximizing J⁡(πθ)J(\pi_{\theta}) via GRPO is consistent with maximizing the underlying information content I~​(πθ)\tilde{I}(\pi_{\theta}), and the divisive normalizer |𝒢|⋅T|\mathcal{G}|\cdot T realizes an adaptive Information-Bottleneck multiplier βeff=1/(|𝒢|⋅T)\beta_{\text{eff}}=1/(|\mathcal{G}|\cdot T) without per-dataset tuning.

E.1 Regularity Conditions

We make these (mild) assumptions:

(A1)

Oracle–policy decoupling. The frozen oracle 𝒪\mathcal{O} depends on 𝒢\mathcal{G} only through its serialization ser⁡(𝒢)\mathrm{ser}(\mathcal{G}), i.e., log⁡P𝒪​(a∗∣q,𝒢)=log⁡P𝒪​(a∗∣q,ser⁡(𝒢))\log P_{\mathcal{O}}(a^{*}\mid q,\mathcal{G})=\log P_{\mathcal{O}}(a^{*}\mid q,\mathrm{ser}(\mathcal{G})). Holds by construction.

(A2)

Per-triple bounded gain. ∃K≥1\exists K\geq 1 such that for any triple tt added to context G<tG_{<t}, I(t;a∗∣q,G<t)≤logKI(t;a^{*}\mid q,G_{<t})\leq\log K nats. Each chunk carries finite information.

(A3)

Format-trained equilibrium. After a brief warm-up Rfmt​(τ)=1R_{\text{fmt}}(\tau)=1 holds on ≥99%\geq 99\% of trajectories (empirically by step 5).

(A4)

Oracle-informative regime. For trained policies, the trajectory distribution concentrates on PMI⁡(𝒢;a∗∣q)≥0\mathrm{PMI}(\mathcal{G};a^{*}\mid q)\geq 0 with high probability. Empirically validated by per-step training logs.

E.2 Proof of the Bounded Monotone Surrogate Property

Define X⁡(𝒢)≔PMI⁡(𝒢;a∗∣q)/(|𝒢|​T)X(\mathcal{G})\coloneqq\mathrm{PMI}(\mathcal{G};a^{*}\mid q)/(|\mathcal{G}|\,T). By (A3), conditional on Rfmt=1R_{\text{fmt}}=1 the IDR contribution is σ⁡(X⁡(𝒢))\sigma(X(\mathcal{G})).

Step 1: Pointwise monotonicity.

σ:ℝ→(0,1)\sigma:\mathbb{R}\to(0,1) is strictly increasing with derivative σ′​(x)=σ⁡(x)​(1−σ⁡(x))∈(0,1/4]\sigma^{\prime}(x)=\sigma(x)(1-\sigma(x))\in(0,1/4]. For any pair 𝒢1,𝒢2\mathcal{G}_{1},\mathcal{G}_{2} under the same (q,a∗)(q,a^{*}),

X⁡(𝒢1)>X⁡(𝒢2)⇔σ⁡(X⁡(𝒢1))>σ⁡(X⁡(𝒢2)).X(\mathcal{G}_{1})>X(\mathcal{G}_{2})\iff\sigma(X(\mathcal{G}_{1}))>\sigma(X(\mathcal{G}_{2})).

Step 2: Jensen bound on the oracle-informative support.

By (A4), the policy’s support concentrates on ℝ≥0\mathbb{R}_{\geq 0}, where σ\sigma is concave (σ′′​(x)=σ′​(x)​(1−2​σ​(x))<0\sigma^{\prime\prime}(x)=\sigma^{\prime}(x)(1-2\sigma(x))<0 for x>0x>0). Jensen’s inequality yields

J⁡(πθ)=𝔼πθ​[σ⁡(X⁡(𝒢))]≤σ⁡(𝔼πθ​[X⁡(𝒢)])=σ⁡(I~​(πθ)),J(\pi_{\theta})=\mathbb{E}_{\pi_{\theta}}[\sigma(X(\mathcal{G}))]\;\leq\;\sigma(\mathbb{E}_{\pi_{\theta}}[X(\mathcal{G})])=\sigma(\tilde{I}(\pi_{\theta})),

where I~​(πθ)≔𝔼πθ​[X⁡(𝒢)]\tilde{I}(\pi_{\theta})\coloneqq\mathbb{E}_{\pi_{\theta}}[X(\mathcal{G})] is the policy expectation of the size-normalized per-trajectory PMI rate; the IT identity 𝔼πθ​[PMI⁡(𝒢;a∗∣q)]=I⁡(𝒢;a∗∣q)\mathbb{E}_{\pi_{\theta}}[\mathrm{PMI}(\mathcal{G};a^{*}\mid q)]=I(\mathcal{G};a^{*}\mid q) then justifies interpreting I~\tilde{I} as the size-normalized conditional-MI rate of πθ\pi_{\theta}’s induced distribution. Equality in the Jensen step holds iff X⁡(𝒢)X(\mathcal{G}) is constant under πθ\pi_{\theta}. Inverting,

I~​(πθ)≥σ−1​(J⁡(πθ))=log⁡J⁡(πθ)1−J⁡(πθ),\tilde{I}(\pi_{\theta})\;\geq\;\sigma^{-1}(J(\pi_{\theta}))\;=\;\log\!\frac{J(\pi_{\theta})}{1-J(\pi_{\theta})},

so high JJ certifies high size-normalized CMI.

Step 3: Bounded Lipschitz signal for GRPO.

σ′​(x)∈(0,1/4]\sigma^{\prime}(x)\in(0,1/4] implies any single trajectory’s contribution to the group-relative advantage estimator under GRPO is 1/41/4-Lipschitz in XX, regardless of how extreme that trajectory’s raw PMI\mathrm{PMI} value is. This eliminates the gradient-explosion failure mode observed in early experiments with unbounded Δ​log⁡p\Delta\log p rewards. □\square

E.3 Information-Bottleneck Connection: Divisive vs. Subtractive

The standard IB objective is subtractive: ℒIB​(πθ)=I⁡(𝒢;a∗∣q)−β​I​(𝒢,X)\mathcal{L}_{\text{IB}}(\pi_{\theta})=I(\mathcal{G};a^{*}\mid q)-\beta\,I(\mathcal{G};X), trading task accuracy against representation complexity. IDR replaces this with the divisive form I⁡(𝒢;a∗∣q)/(|𝒢|​T)I(\mathcal{G};a^{*}\mid q)/(|\mathcal{G}|\,T), yielding three advantages.

(i) Adaptive βeff\beta_{\text{eff}}.

By (A2) and the chain rule of mutual information, I⁡(𝒢,X)≤|𝒢|​log⁡KI(\mathcal{G};X)\leq|\mathcal{G}|\log K, so

I⁡(𝒢;a∗∣q)|𝒢|​T≤log⁡KT⋅I⁡(𝒢;a∗∣q)I⁡(𝒢,X);\frac{I(\mathcal{G};a^{*}\mid q)}{|\mathcal{G}|\,T}\;\leq\;\frac{\log K}{T}\cdot\frac{I(\mathcal{G};a^{*}\mid q)}{I(\mathcal{G};X)};

the divisive form is bounded above by a constant multiple of the IB ratio I⁡(𝒢;a∗∣q)/I⁡(𝒢,X)I(\mathcal{G};a^{*}\mid q)/I(\mathcal{G};X), with constant log⁡K/T\log K/T that depends only on the per-triple alphabet and the temperature, not on the dataset. Equivalently, the divisive form realizes an adaptive Lagrange multiplier βeff=1/(|𝒢|​T)\beta_{\text{eff}}=1/(|\mathcal{G}|\,T) that scales with graph size: larger graphs face proportionally higher information-density bars without per-dataset hand-tuning of β\beta.

(ii) Bounded gradients.

Subtractive IB rewards are unbounded; the σ\sigma-wrapped divisive form bounds reward to [−1,1][-1,1] and gradient contribution to 1/41/4-Lipschitz, simplifying GRPO training.

(iii) Relation to standard IB.

IDR is motivated by IB rather than algebraically equivalent: divisive normalization saturates at large PMI\mathrm{PMI}, while subtractive IB does not. The divisive form is chosen for the gradient-stability and adaptive-β\beta properties above.

E.4 Strict Subgraph Monotonicity

Informative triples are strictly rewarded.

For 𝒢2⊊𝒢1\mathcal{G}_{2}\subsetneq\mathcal{G}_{1} with I(𝒢1∖𝒢2;a∗∣q,𝒢2)>0I(\mathcal{G}_{1}\setminus\mathcal{G}_{2};a^{*}\mid q,\mathcal{G}_{2})>0, the chain rule of mutual information gives PMI⁡(𝒢1)>PMI⁡(𝒢2)\mathrm{PMI}(\mathcal{G}_{1})>\mathrm{PMI}(\mathcal{G}_{2}). Combined with strict σ\sigma monotonicity, RIDR​(𝒢1)>RIDR​(𝒢2)R_{\textsc{IDR}}(\mathcal{G}_{1})>R_{\textsc{IDR}}(\mathcal{G}_{2}).

Uninformative triples are strictly penalized.

For 𝒢2⊊𝒢1\mathcal{G}_{2}\subsetneq\mathcal{G}_{1} with I(𝒢1∖𝒢2;a∗∣q,𝒢2)=0I(\mathcal{G}_{1}\setminus\mathcal{G}_{2};a^{*}\mid q,\mathcal{G}_{2})=0, PMI⁡(𝒢1)=PMI⁡(𝒢2)\mathrm{PMI}(\mathcal{G}_{1})=\mathrm{PMI}(\mathcal{G}_{2}) but |𝒢1|>|𝒢2||\mathcal{G}_{1}|>|\mathcal{G}_{2}|, so X⁡(𝒢1)<X⁡(𝒢2)X(\mathcal{G}_{1})<X(\mathcal{G}_{2}) and RIDR​(𝒢1)<RIDR​(𝒢2)R_{\textsc{IDR}}(\mathcal{G}_{1})<R_{\textsc{IDR}}(\mathcal{G}_{2}). This formalizes the “minimum sufficient subgraph” inductive bias: the policy is strictly incentivized to include triples carrying information about a∗a^{*} and only those.

E.5 Asymmetric Coverage: Bounds and Random-Trajectory Baseline

This subsection records two mathematical facts about the asymmetric coverage function 𝒞⁡(τ,P)≔|A⁡(τ)∩σP|/|σP|\mathcal{C}(\tau,P)\coloneqq|A(\tau)\cap\sigma_{P}|/|\sigma_{P}| that we use in the PAR reward (Eq. 5). They are not used in the proof of Theorem 1 but justify two choices reflected in the experiments.

Proposition (range and tightness).

For any trajectory τ\tau producing the abstract triple set A⁡(τ)A(\tau) and any pattern PP with skeleton σP\sigma_{P} of size m≔|σP|m\coloneqq|\sigma_{P}|,

𝒞⁡(τ,P)∈[0,1],𝒞⁡(τ,P)=1⇔σP⊆A⁡(τ).\mathcal{C}(\tau,P)\in[0,1],\qquad\mathcal{C}(\tau,P)=1\iff\sigma_{P}\subseteq A(\tau). (11)

Furthermore, when |A⁡(τ)|=k|A(\tau)|=k and k≥mk\geq m, the coverage admits the lower bound

𝒞⁡(τ,P)≥k∩m,k∩≔|A⁡(τ)∩σP|,\mathcal{C}(\tau,P)\geq\frac{k_{\cap}}{m},\qquad k_{\cap}\coloneqq|A(\tau)\cap\sigma_{P}|, (12)

with equality iff every triple in σP\sigma_{P} matches at most one triple in A⁡(τ)A(\tau) under the chosen type abstraction. The asymmetry of 𝒞\mathcal{C} (skeleton size in the denominator, not |A||A|) follows directly: adding non-matching triples to τ\tau does not penalize coverage, which is the property we use at training time to allow the policy to explore beyond the retrieved skeleton without paying a coverage cost.

Corollary (random-trajectory baseline).

Let UU be the universe of distinct typed triples induced by the type abstraction and the relation vocabulary, and let τ\tau be a trajectory drawn uniformly at random over abstract triple sets of size kk. The expected coverage of any fixed skeleton σP\sigma_{P} of size mm is

𝔼τ[𝒞(τ,P)]=k|U|,Pr[𝒞(τ,P)=1]=(km)(|U|m)−1,\mathbb{E}_{\tau}[\mathcal{C}(\tau,P)]=\frac{k}{|U|},\qquad\Pr[\mathcal{C}(\tau,P)=1]=\binom{k}{m}\binom{|U|}{m}^{-1}, (13)

which is exponentially small in mm for k≪|U|k\ll|U|. Concretely, with |U|≈4⋅104|U|\approx 4\cdot 10^{4} in our paper-main configuration (entity-types squared ×\times relation count), k=3k=3 (typical trajectory length), and m=2.5m=2.5 (average skeleton length, Table 16), the random-trajectory baseline is 𝔼⁡[𝒞]≈7.5×10−5\mathbb{E}[\mathcal{C}]\approx 7.5\times 10^{-5} and the exact-match probability is below 10−810^{-8}. The empirical RPF in Table 3 (0.8860.886) and the empirical GPM-CEM (0.0990.099) thus exceed the random baseline by roughly 44 and 66 orders of magnitude respectively, ruling out the alternative explanation that PB trajectories happen to overlap with stored skeletons by chance.

G.1 Metric Reading Guide

Table 6 consolidates the metrics referenced throughout §4, with definitions, direction (higher- or lower-is-better), and the table or figure where each metric is reported.

G.2 Hypergraph Index Construction

The hypergraph index H=(V,Ehyper,Xtext)H=(V,E_{\text{hyper}},X_{\text{text}}) that supports both Stage I and Stage II is built once, offline, before any RL training and shared across all stages and seeds. We adopt the construction protocol of Graph-R1 [6] and HippoRAG [12], which we summarize here for self-containment; configurations match the reproduction settings.

Step 1: Corpus chunking.

The retrieval corpus 𝒞\mathcal{C} is the FlashRAG [45] Wiki-2018 dump (21 015 32421\,015\,324 passages). Each passage is tokenized with the default GPT-2 tokenizer and split into fixed-length chunks of 100100 tokens with no overlap, following the FlashRAG default and the Search-R1 baseline configuration. Chunk boundaries are aligned to the nearest sentence end so that no sentence spans two chunks; the resulting chunk count is ∼26 012 000\sim 26\,012\,000. We retain the original chunk text XtextX_{\text{text}} for display; the agent’s ⟨query⟩\langle\textsf{query}\rangle block returns top-55 hyperedges and their associated chunks.

Step 2: Entity and relation extraction.

For each chunk we issue one prompted call to gpt-4o-mini [46] that returns a list of ⟨entity,relation,entity⟩\langle\textsf{entity},\textsf{relation},\textsf{entity}\rangle triples together with a short natural-language fact summary. The extraction prompt follows Graph-R1 verbatim; we cache all extractions on disk (LMDB) and amortize construction over a single ∼18\sim 18-hour run on 3232 CPU workers, costing ∼$210{\sim}\$210 in API credits one time. Entities are normalized via lowercasing and Unicode-NFKC; relations are kept as free-form predicate strings (typical length 11–33 tokens, no fixed schema). The extraction yields ∼41\sim 41\,M unique entities and ∼87\sim 87\,M raw triples.

Step 3: Hyperedge formation.

Each chunk’s facts are bundled into a single hyperedge that connects all of the chunk’s mentioned entities; the chunk’s text becomes the hyperedge’s content payload. Formally, hyperedge e∈Ehypere\in E_{\text{hyper}} is a tuple (eents⊆V,etext∈Xtext)(e_{\text{ents}}\subseteq V,e_{\text{text}}\in X_{\text{text}}), where eentse_{\text{ents}} is the set of entities mentioned in the chunk and etexte_{\text{text}} is the chunk text. Entity–passage incidence is therefore implicitly captured: an entity v∈Vv\in V participates in every hyperedge whose chunk mentions vv. We do not maintain a separate entity–sentence relation; sentence-level granularity is collapsed into the chunk-level hyperedge so that the retrieval unit matches the chunk granularity used by all baselines.

Step 4: Dense index.

Hyperedges are encoded with BGE-large-en-v1.5 [44]: the embedding input is the concatenation of the hyperedge’s fact summaries followed by the chunk text, capped at 512512 tokens. The resulting 10241024-dim vectors are stored in a FAISS IndexHNSWFlat [36] index (M=32M=32, ef_construction =100=100) for sub-millisecond top-kk retrieval at agent runtime. The full index occupies ∼102\sim 102 GB on disk; we serve it from a CPU-resident in-memory index on the retriever node (no GPU needed at inference).

Step 5: Retrieval interface.

At every ⟨query⟩\langle\textsf{query}\rangle block from the agent, the retrieval service receives a free-form query string, encodes it once with the same BGE-large encoder, and returns the top-k=5k=5 hyperedges (default for all methods we compare to). The return payload contains both the hyperedge’s entity set eentse_{\text{ents}} and its chunk text etexte_{\text{text}}, presented to the agent in a fixed template. The same retrieval interface and same k=5k=5 budget are used at training and at deployment.

Offline vs. online split.

Table 7 summarizes which steps run once-and-cached versus per-query. The hypergraph index, the FAISS encoder, and the GPM are all offline artifacts: they are built once per corpus and frozen for both Stage I and Stage II training as well as deployment-time inference. The oracle is consumed only at Stage I training, after which it is discarded; the policy and FAISS retriever are the only components invoked at deployment time.

We contrast the two evidence-graph representations relevant to PatternBloom: a binary knowledge graph (the substrate adopted by KG-based RAG methods such as HippoRAG, GraphRAG, GFM-RAG, LinearRAG, and LightRAG) and a hypergraph (the substrate adopted by Graph-R1, HypergraphRAG, and PatternBloom). Both representations are constructed once and cached. The operational difference is what the agent receives per call: a single binary triple in the KG case, versus a hyperedge plus its associated chunk text in the hypergraph case. The hypergraph payload is therefore a self-contained piece of context (one chunk’s worth of facts about a co-mentioned set of entities), whereas the binary KG defers the burden of recovering chunk-level context to the agent. Paragraph-based methods (Search-R1, FrugalRAG, R1-Searcher) do not construct an evidence graph at all; they retrieve raw passages directly and are outside the scope of this comparison.

G.3 Inference Pipeline

At deployment, given an input query qq, PatternBloom runs four steps (Figure 2, bottom).

(1) Signature extraction. The query signature σ⁡(q)\sigma(q) is extracted by the deterministic parser of §3.3 and embedded into a BGE-large vector.

(2) Pattern retrieval. The frozen ℳ0\mathcal{M}_{0} is queried via FAISS cosine retrieval; the top-33 patterns whose signature similarity exceeds θsim=0.5\theta_{\mathrm{sim}}=0.5 are formatted as a single ⟨knowledge⟩\langle\textsf{knowledge}\rangle hint and prepended to the agent’s prompt. If no pattern clears θsim\theta_{\mathrm{sim}}, no hint is injected and the agent proceeds with the standard multi-hop tool instructions in the system prompt.

(3) Trajectory rollout. The deployed policy πθ2∗\pi_{\theta^{*}_{2}} performs an interleaved ⟨think⟩\langle\textsf{think}\rangle/⟨query⟩\langle\textsf{query}\rangle/⟨graph⟩\langle\textsf{graph}\rangle/⟨answer⟩\langle\textsf{answer}\rangle rollout over the same hypergraph index HH used at training time; each ⟨query⟩\langle\textsf{query}\rangle block triggers a retriever call that returns the top-kk matching hyperedges, and the agent accumulates 𝒢\mathcal{G} across turns.

(4) Answer extraction. The final ⟨answer⟩\langle\textsf{answer}\rangle block is extracted as the model output. The oracle 𝒪\mathcal{O} and gradient updates from training are not used at inference; the deployment cost is therefore equal to a standard agentic-RAG rollout plus a single FAISS lookup against the |ℳ0||\mathcal{M}_{0}|-entry pattern memory.

G.4 Cost-Quality Trade-off

Table 8 compares PatternBloom against representative methods spanning two retrieval paradigms (LLM-extracted KG, in GFM-RAG and LightRAG; adaptive structure, in StructRAG) on one-time indexing cost and downstream retrieval quality. GFM-RAG and LightRAG values are reproduced from LinearRAG [14]’s efficiency analysis on the same 2WikiMultiHopQA corpus; PatternBloom’s value is computed from our own 2WikiMultiHopQA build artifacts (extraction template, chunk content, and produced entity/hyperedge output); StructRAG performs all LLM work at query time, and the value reflects total LLM tokens summed over the 1,0001{,}000 test queries on 2WikiMultiHopQA rather than a one-time index. PatternBloom attains the strongest retrieval quality across all paradigms, with R@5 86.686.6 and EvR 72.072.0 averaged over the four multi-hop benchmarks, exceeding the strongest non-RL baseline GFM-RAG by +5.3+5.3 R@5 and +4.0+4.0 EvR. The nn-ary hyperedge construction underlying PatternBloom consumes 31.131.1M LLM tokens on 2WikiMultiHopQA: 36%36\% of LightRAG’s 86.786.7M (dual-level KG with high- and low-level community reports), and 7.8×7.8\times the lightweight GFM-RAG triple-extraction pipeline, trading the cheaper triple regime for substantially higher recall. Once constructed, the hypergraph is reused across all queries, so the one-time indexing cost amortizes to zero per-query overhead at deployment, while every query in training-free baselines such as GFM-RAG continues to incur GPT-4o-mini API calls. The combined view positions PatternBloom on the construction-cost-versus-retrieval-recall Pareto frontier: lighter KG pipelines save tokens at the price of weaker recall, and LightRAG consumes 2.8×2.8\times more tokens than PatternBloom without reporting comparable retrieval quality. These numbers substantiate the architectural claim of §1 from the deployment side: a one-time hypergraph build amortizes across queries, and procedural memory contributes the gains in Table 1 at no additional per-query API cost.

G.5 Multi-Size Scaling

The multi-size scaling of PatternBloom is reported in Table 1 of the main body, panels (b), (c), (d), and (e) for Qwen2.5-7B, Qwen3-8B, Qwen2.5-14B, and Qwen2.5-32B respectively. Three observations follow. First, PatternBloom ranks first within every size panel on the Avg-IID and Avg-OOD summary columns. Second, within the Qwen2.5 family the gain from 77B to 1414B is +5.3+5.3 EM and from 1414B to 3232B is +2.9+2.9 EM, indicating diminishing returns past the 1414B parameter band. Third, PatternBloom (Q3-8B) attains the highest Avg-OOD (43.443.4 EM) among all 88B entries in panel (c), ahead of Search-R1, Graph-R1, FrugalRAG, and R1 at the same parameter count, confirming that the procedural-memory mechanism transfers across backbone families and is not tied to the Qwen2.5 line.

G.6 Per-Paper Settings and IID/OOD Definitions

Reported numbers in Table 1 come from baselines that span four training paradigms: (i) RL-trained agentic search, (ii) zero-shot prompting on a strong reasoning backbone, (iii) prompt-engineered RAG over a frozen instruction-tuned LLM, and (iv) training-free retrieval pipelines. Within each paradigm, training corpora differ from paper to paper, so the IID/OOD partition of our seven test datasets differs across rows. We mark IID/OOD in Table 1 according to our training set (HotpotQA ++ 2WikiMHQA), but reported numbers for other methods may reflect their own in-distribution data. We summarize each method’s setting below; the marking (‡ reported, † AceSearcher reproduction) follows the convention of the main-text caption.

(I) RL-trained agentic search (panels b/c/d/e of Tab. 1).

  • •

    PatternBloom (ours, all sizes 1.5B/7B/8B/14B/32B): two-stage RL (IDR Stage I, PAR Stage II) on HotpotQA ++ 2WikiMHQA (1414K total, seed 4242). IID = {HotpotQA, 2WikiMHQA}; OOD = {MuSiQue, Bamboogle, NQ, TriviaQA, PopQA}.

  • •

    Search-R1 (7B/8B/14B)‡ [5]: RL with format-and-EM reward on NQ ++ HotpotQA training mixture. Their IID = {NQ, HotpotQA}; their OOD = {TriviaQA, PopQA, 2WikiMHQA, MuSiQue, Bamboogle}. The reported NQ EM (48.648.6 at 14B) is in-distribution for them but in our OOD column. We use Search-R1-base numbers from Jin et al. [5]’s appendix Table on 14B-LLM scaling.

  • •

    R1-Searcher (7B) [7]: RL on HotpotQA ++ 2WikiMHQA, same training distribution as ours; row in panel (c) is our reproduction.

  • •

    Graph-R1 (7B/8B) [6], Structure-R1 (7B) [18]: RL on HotpotQA ++ 2WikiMHQA. Same training distribution as ours; rows are our reproductions.

    FrugalRAG (7B/8B) [10]: RL on HotpotQA ++ 2WikiMHQA; rows are our reproductions.

    ReSearch (32B Q2.5-32B-Inst)‡ [27]: RL on MuSiQue only. Their IID = {MuSiQue}; their OOD = {HotpotQA, 2WikiMHQA, Bamboogle} (their paper does not evaluate on the three single-hop datasets, hence “–” in panel (e)). Their reported MuSiQue EM (26.426.4) benefits from MuSiQue-only training and is in our OOD column; HotpotQA / 2WikiMHQA / Bamboogle are OOD for both.

(II) Zero-shot prompting on reasoning backbones.

(III) Prompt-engineered RAG over instruction-tuned LLMs (AceSearcher reproduction).

No model parameters are updated, so the IID/OOD distinction does not apply to the agent itself.
