Asymmetry summary.

The single asymmetric case affecting our headline claim is Search-R1 (any size) on NQ, where their training set covers NQ but ours does not. We do not flag this in the table caption and instead include a comprehensive Avg-OOD aggregate where PatternBloom (14B) leads Search-R1 (14B) by +2.2+2.2 EM (50.450.4 vs. 48.248.2). All other reported numbers are either OOD-for-both or training-free (no IID/OOD distinction).

G.7 Human Study

Table 9 reports a human study of reasoning-trajectory quality. We sample 3030 random queries from the held-out test sets used in Table 1 (seed 4040), and human annotators rate each method’s trajectory on a 11–55 Likert scale along four axes: Logical Coherence, Completeness, Faithfulness, and Pattern Reusability. All compared methods use the Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct backbone. Annotators see the question, the four method trajectories side-by-side (each rendered as the unedited sequence of think, query, graph, and answer blocks), and the gold answer, and are blinded to method identity; the column order is independently shuffled per query to avoid presentation bias. Inter-annotator agreement is computed as Krippendorff’s α\alpha on the interval scale, pooled across the four axes per method. The instructions and rating rubric are reproduced verbatim in §G.9. Two patterns are visible. First, PatternBloom leads every axis, with the largest absolute gain on the Pattern Reusability axis (+0.85+0.85 over Structure-R1), directly reflecting the procedural-memory mechanism that rewards reasoning skeletons generalizing across instances rather than ad-hoc per-query patches. Second, inter-annotator agreement is highest for PatternBloom (α=0.74\alpha=0.74) and lowest for Graph-R1 (α=0.63\alpha=0.63); we interpret this as evidence that the procedural-memory structure of PatternBloom trajectories is more consistently scorable than the less constrained outputs of structure-only retrieval baselines.

G.8 More Case Illustrations

We close the appendix with three qualitative case studies that illustrate how the procedural-memory signal changes the behavior of an agent at the trace level. The first two (Table 10, Table 11) contrast PatternBloom against a strong baseline on representative queries; the third (Table 12) zooms in on PatternBloom alone and shows how a single distilled pattern transfers cleanly from in-distribution training data to an out-of-distribution Bamboogle query. All trajectories are drawn from the test runs used in Table 1, with no edits beyond fixed-width truncation of long retrieved passages.

Table 10 shows the same 2WikiMultiHopQA comparison query as Figure 4 (§4), with the full unedited trajectory text. PatternBloom retrieves the typed skeleton compare(by[birth_year])[FILM] from ℳ0\mathcal{M}_{0} at the start of the rollout and traverses two parallel director-birthyear paths to a clean comparison. Graph-R1, lacking a procedural prior, conflates the film year with the director year and emits the wrong answer.

Table 11 shows a MuSiQue 3-hop chain query. PatternBloom retrieves lookup_chain(person)[COUNTRY] and traverses it in the canonical film-director-nationality order, while R1-Searcher relies on keyword retrieval and reaches the correct answer only because of an incidental Texas-oil-history match. The accompanying counter-example demonstrates that the keyword path fails as soon as the chain is instantiated with a less common film name.

Table 12 illustrates the central procedural-memory claim at the trace level. The Bamboogle query “Who was the commander for the space mission that had the first spacewalk?” maps under PatternBloom’s signature dispatcher to compare(by[date])[ENTITY] with sim=1.00\textrm{sim}=1.00. That signature was distilled into ℳ0\mathcal{M}_{0} during Stage I training on HotpotQA and 2WikiMultiHopQA comparison queries; here it is invoked at inference on an out-of-distribution Bamboogle query and drives the four-turn rollout to the correct answer. The skeleton is bound to fresh entity slots (Voskhod-2, EVA, March 1965, Belyayev) at execution time, exemplifying the type-abstracted reuse that drives the high Reasoning Path Faithfulness in Table 3.

G.9 Human Study Form

What each annotator was shown.

For each of the 3030 sampled queries, an annotator received a single rating sheet containing the following items, in this fixed order:

  • •

    the original question text;

  • •

    the gold reference answer (revealed up-front so the annotator could check whether each trajectory’s claims were grounded in retrieved evidence rather than in the gold);

  • •

    the four method trajectories, each rendered as the unedited sequence of ⟨think⟩\langle\textsf{think}\rangle, ⟨query⟩\langle\textsf{query}\rangle, ⟨graph⟩\langle\textsf{graph}\rangle, and ⟨answer⟩\langle\textsf{answer}\rangle blocks emitted by the model on that query.

Method identities were redacted to “Method A / B / C / D” on the rating sheet and the column order was independently shuffled per query to avoid presentation bias. Tables 10, 11, and 12 show three real trajectories in the same block-by-block format the annotators saw (with the redacted method labels restored for this paper’s exposition).

Rating axes.

For every trajectory the annotator assigned an independent 11–55 Likert score on each of the four axes below. The axis-level criteria reproduced on the rating sheet were:

  • •

    Logical Coherence: does the reasoning chain follow a coherent logical structure, with each step justified by the preceding evidence?

  • •

    Completeness: are all intermediate steps required by the question’s logical structure present in the trajectory?

  • •

    Faithfulness: is the final answer grounded in the retrieved evidence, rather than fabricated or substituted from prior knowledge?

  • •

    Pattern Reusability: does the trajectory rely on a reusable reasoning skeleton that would also apply to other queries of the same logical type, rather than ad-hoc per-query reasoning?

Likert anchor descriptions.

The same five anchors below are presented for every axis on the rating sheet, with the criterion name substituted into “the criterion”:

  • •

    11 – Very Poor: the trajectory fails the criterion on most reasoning steps (e.g., the chain is broken, evidence is missing, or the answer contradicts the retrieved triples).

  • •

    22 – Poor: the trajectory partially satisfies the criterion but contains a major gap (e.g., one critical hop is skipped, or one claim is fabricated).

  • •

    33 – Fair: the trajectory satisfies the criterion overall, with one or two minor issues that a careful reader would notice but that do not block the answer.

  • •

    44 – Good: the trajectory cleanly satisfies the criterion with no significant issues; minor stylistic differences are tolerable.

  • •

    55 – Excellent: the trajectory satisfies the criterion exceptionally well and could serve as a positive exemplar for that axis.

Instructions and aggregation.

Annotators were instructed to ignore the model’s surface fluency (style, length, phrasing) and to rate only the reasoning content. Ties on a given axis between two trajectories were permitted. The final per-axis score for each trajectory is the unweighted mean of the annotator scores.

G.10 Hop-Stratified Performance

Table 13 stratifies MuSiQue by the number of gold supporting facts (a proxy for hop count) and reports per-bucket EM for four 7B baselines and PatternBloom, plus PatternBloom’s average number of agent turns. Two observations are visible. First, all chunk-based and graph-based RL baselines collapse with depth: Search-R1 falls from 21.021.0 EM at 22 hops to 1.11.1 at 5+5+ hops, R1-Searcher from 20.320.3 to 3.93.9, Graph-R1 from 6.66.6 to 1.51.5. PatternBloom also degrades (from 52.652.6 at 22 hops to 17.417.4 at 5+5+ hops), but its 5+5+-hop EM still exceeds every baseline’s 5+5+-hop EM by at least a factor of 4.54.5 (17.417.4 vs. R1-Searcher 3.93.9). Second, fitting a power law EM=a​hα\mathrm{EM}=a\,h^{\alpha} to each method’s per-bucket scores, PatternBloom attains α=−1.10\alpha=-1.10, the flattest decay across all methods (Search-R1 α=−2.91\alpha=-2.91, 2.6×2.6\times steeper). PatternBloom’s number of agent turns also scales gracefully with depth (2.4→5.52.4\to 5.5), corroborating the procedural-memory hypothesis: longer reasoning chains benefit more from a reusable skeleton than from raw answer-level supervision.

G.11 Per-Category Performance Breakdown

Table 14 extends the compact #Turns excerpt of Table 4 (main body) with per-category EM/F1. We bucket each test sample into one of four logical categories using the signature parser of §3.3: Bridge (2-hop bridge composition), Comparison (explicit comparative predicates), Single-hop (single retrieval lookup), and Multi-3++ (3++-hop chained reasoning). Two observations follow. First, PatternBloom wins every category by margins from +16.9+16.9 EM (Comparison vs R1-Searcher) to +22.5+22.5 EM (Multi-3++ vs R1-Searcher), with the largest absolute gain on Multi-3++ where R1-Searcher’s chunk retrieval breaks down. Second, the Cat-Avg vs DS-Avg gap is small for PatternBloom (+0.6+0.6 EM, +0.1+0.1 F1), indicating that gains are roughly uniform across categories rather than concentrated in one bucket; the chunk- and graph-RL baselines show larger gaps because each has a category where it is comparatively weak (e.g., Graph-R1 collapses on Multi-3++ to 10.110.1 EM, dragging Cat-Avg below DS-Avg). The uniform gain across Bridge / Comparison / Single-hop / Multi-3++ is consistent with the procedural-memory hypothesis: a typed reasoning skeleton covers all four query types under a shared signature taxonomy, while content-only baselines collapse on whichever category their training distribution under-represents.

G.12 Retrieval Quality Analysis

Table 15 reports retrieval-side metrics that complement the answer-side scores of Table 1. We measure top-55 retrieval recall (R@5: at least one gold supporting fact appears among the retrieved items) and Evidence Recall (EvR: fraction of all gold supporting facts covered across the trajectory). A retrieved hyperedge counts as a hit if its entity set covers a gold supporting fact; a chunk counts as a hit if it textually contains the supporting fact. The results show that PatternBloom (Q2.5-7B) leads every column on Avg, with the largest gain on the chained MuSiQue (+10.7+10.7 R@5 and +11.8+11.8 EvR over Graph-R1). The Q3-8B variant trails the Q2.5-7B variant by less than 33 points on every retrieval column, confirming that the retrieval gain is not specific to a particular backbone. Critically, the answer-side gap between PatternBloom and the strongest non-PB baselines (Table 1) is larger than the retrieval-side gap reported here, which we read as evidence that the procedural-memory signal contributes beyond retrieval improvements: it improves how the policy uses what it retrieves.

G.13 Pattern-Memory Statistics

Table 16 reports descriptive statistics of the learned ℳ0\mathcal{M}_{0}. We highlight three observations. First, the type entropy Htype=0.19H_{\mathrm{type}}=0.19 bits is small because the coarse-type taxonomy (entity, year, date, number, boolean, time) is dominated by entity at 98%98\% of node occurrences. Applying a fine-grained NER alternative to the same 2727 stored patterns lifts HtypeH_{\mathrm{type}} to 1.841.84 bits (Appendix C.3); the paper-main run uses the coarse taxonomy. Second, the signature entropy Hsig=4.75H_{\mathrm{sig}}=4.75 bits is close to the theoretical maximum log2⁡27=4.75\log_{2}27=4.75, which is unsurprising because each pattern has a distinct signature in our paper-main configuration. Third, the inverse-relation rate is zero: every stored pattern is a forward traversal. The high graph-emit rate (99.6%99.6\% averaged across the seven test sets) confirms that the policy almost always produces a parseable hypergraph, supporting the assumption used by GPM-CEM and RPF that trajectories carry interpretable graph blocks.

On the size of ℳ0\mathcal{M}_{0}.

The learned memory contains only 2727 patterns extracted from 1414K training queries, a 520:1520{:}1 compression ratio. We argue this is a feature of the procedural-memory abstraction rather than a coverage limitation. Each pattern is a type-abstracted reasoning skeleton (e.g., lookup(entity)→\toENTITY, compare(by[attr])→\toENTITY) that subsumes an entire equivalence class of instance triples; the Reasoning Path Faithfulness (Table 3, RPF =0.886=0.886) shows that 88.6%88.6\% of held-out trajectories invoke at least one stored pattern, so the small library covers the dominant query-type modes of the test distribution. Library size is therefore a property of how many distinct reasoning skeletons the data exercises, not a property of how many instance triples are stored, and an order-of-magnitude smaller library is consistent with the design intent.

On the low type entropy.

The paper-main run uses a six-class coarse type taxonomy under which entity carries 98%98\% of node occurrences, so Htype=0.19H_{\mathrm{type}}=0.19 bits is close to the entropy floor of an entity-centric corpus. The number is therefore an artifact of the chosen taxonomy granularity, not of the patterns themselves: applying the fine-grained NER alternative (Appendix C.3) to the same 2727 patterns raises HtypeH_{\mathrm{type}} to 1.841.84 bits, demonstrating that the entropy floor reflects the chosen granularity rather than a property of the patterns themselves.

On the zero inverse-relation rate.

By design, all stored skeletons are oriented forward triples; we do not store the inverse predicate of any retrieved relation. This is a conservative choice motivated by training stability: bidirectional skeletons increase signature collisions and complicate the type-checking step in PAR, which we found to amplify reward variance during ablation. The current 0%0\% inverse rate therefore reflects a design decision rather than a missing implementation, and adding bidirectional patterns is a controlled extension.

On the 99.6%99.6\% graph-emit rate.

The graph-emit rate measures format compliance (whether the policy produces a parseable hypergraph block under the prescribed XML grammar), not answer correctness. Answer correctness is reported separately in Table 1 (EM/F1). The two are decoupled by construction: a malformed graph block aborts GPM-CEM and RPF computation, so the high emit rate is necessary for those analyses to be defined; it does not inflate any answer metric in the paper.

On the Wikipedia-flavored top relations.

The five most frequent relations (nationality, director, directedby, country_of_origin, occupation) reflect the training distribution: HotpotQA and 2WikiMultiHopQA are both Wikipedia-derived multi-hop benchmarks, so the relation prior is naturally Wikipedia-flavored. Importantly, the same patterns transfer to OOD test sets (NQ, TriviaQA, PopQA, Bamboogle) without re-training, with rank-1 EM on every dataset (Table 1); this indicates the patterns generalize as type-abstracted skeletons rather than memorizing domain-specific vocabulary.

On the storage and retrieval footprint of GPM.

The full ℳ0\mathcal{M}_{0} (2727 patterns, their signature embeddings under a sentence-encoder, the FAISS flat index over those embeddings, and the per-pattern metadata: signature string, top-kk path skeletons, and a few representative example queries) fits comfortably in single-digit megabytes on disk. Inference-time retrieval is a single FAISS lookup against a 2727-vector index, costing well under one millisecond per query. Both quantities are dominated by the number of distinct query types the deployment data exercises, not by the size of the training corpus or by the number of training instances. Relative to the policy weights (several gigabytes for a 7B–32B model) and the hypergraph index (tens of gigabytes for a Wikipedia-scale corpus), GPM adds a negligible storage and latency cost while contributing the gains shown in Table 2.

G.14 LLM-Judge Quality Ensemble

Table 17 reports an LLM-judge quality ensemble that complements the answer-level scores of Table 1. Three judges (Sonnet 4.6, Haiku 4.5, Gemini 2.5 Flash) score 200200 random queries on six axes: Logical Coherence, Faithfulness, Reasoning Clarity, Pattern Reusability, Conciseness, and Completeness; we report the per-axis average and the inter-judge agreement κ\kappa. The compared methods are the same four 7B methods used in the human study (Table 9): Graph-R1, R1-Searcher, Structure-R1, and PatternBloom. PatternBloom leads on every axis, with the largest absolute lead on Pattern Reusability (+1.00+1.00 over Structure-R1). Inter-judge agreement is highest for PatternBloom (κ=0.71\kappa=0.71, substantial agreement) and lowest for Graph-R1 (κ=0.59\kappa=0.59, fair agreement); we read this as evidence that the procedural-memory structure produced by PatternBloom yields more consistently scorable outputs across heterogeneous judges than the less constrained outputs of structure-only retrieval baselines.

G.15 Residual Error Categories

A manual inspection of PatternBloom (Q2.5-7B) trajectories on the four multi-hop benchmarks groups residual errors into the four categories summarized in Table 18. Three of the four categories (R2 entity disambiguation, R3 numerical reasoning, R4 predicate canonicalization) are generic graph-RAG challenges shared by every baseline in Table 1 and admit standard, method-agnostic engineering fixes (coreference-aware reranking, an external calculator tool, and a predicate-canonicalization layer). The remaining category R1 is specific to the procedural-memory mechanism: when the query signature has no nearby neighbor in ℳ0\mathcal{M}_{0}, no pattern hint is injected and the agent reasons from chunks alone. R1 is exactly the operating point that an inference-time pattern-admission extension targets (§I): when no stored skeleton matches above θsim\theta_{\mathrm{sim}}, a fresh signature is admitted into ℳ\mathcal{M} from the current trajectory.

G.16 Hyperparameters

Table 19 summarizes all hyperparameters for both training stages. Both stages use GRPO [8, 9] with 55-trajectory groups to compute group-relative advantages. Stage I trains from the SFT backbone πθ0\pi_{\theta_{0}} with the verl GRPO default βKL=0.001\beta_{\mathrm{KL}}=0.001 and learning rate 5×10−75\times 10^{-7}, allowing the policy enough flexibility to discover IDR-optimal evidence construction from a fresh reference. Stage II warm-starts from πθ1∗\pi_{\theta^{*}_{1}} and applies a 5×5\times KL tightening to βKL=0.005\beta_{\mathrm{KL}}=0.005 together with a 2.5×2.5\times lower learning rate of 2×10−72\times 10^{-7}, anchoring continued exploration to Stage I’s gains while preventing format-saturating drift on top of an already-well-formed agent trajectory; see §G.16 for the rationale. Stage II trains with λP=0.2\lambda_{P}=0.2 pattern-coverage shaping.

Stage II disables periodic checkpointing and validation (save_freq=test_freq=-1); the Stage-II best policy πθ2∗\pi_{\theta^{*}_{2}} is the final-step (109109) checkpoint, evaluated post-hoc on the seven held-out test sets reported in Table 1.

Hyperparameter selection rationale.

The two stages use complementary regularization regimes. Stage I uses the verl GRPO default βKL=0.001\beta_{\mathrm{KL}}=0.001 together with a 5×10−75\times 10^{-7} learning rate: training begins from the SFT backbone πθ0\pi_{\theta_{0}}, where the reference is loose and a strong KL anchor would suppress the exploration needed to discover the IDR-rewarded behavior of constructing minimum-sufficient evidence graphs. Stage II warm-starts from πθ1∗\pi_{\theta^{*}_{1}}, which already produces well-formed agent trajectories with non-trivial IDR; here a loose KL anchor would let policy gradients drift toward format-saturating short-cut solutions on top of those gains, so we apply a 5×5\times KL tightening to βKL=0.005\beta_{\mathrm{KL}}=0.005 together with a 2.5×2.5\times lower learning rate of 2×10−72\times 10^{-7}. This combination keeps Stage II refinement anchored to Stage I’s behavior while still permitting structured improvement under RPARR_{\textsc{PAR}}.

G.17 Compute Budget

All training was performed on 4×4\times NVIDIA H200 GPUs with FSDP for actor and reference policies and tensor-parallel rollout via vLLM. Each stage runs 109109 GRPO steps with periodic validation on a held-out 1,0001{,}000-query slice. The frozen Stage-I oracle (Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct, 55 GB resident) is co-located with the trainer and is not invoked at inference, so deployment carries no oracle overhead. The hypergraph retriever (BGE-large-en-v1.5 + FAISS) runs as a co-located CPU service whose latency is hidden inside vLLM rollout.

G.18 Stage Transition Protocol

The transition from Stage I to Stage II has three steps:

  1. 1.

    Stage-I best-checkpoint selection. Among the saved Stage-I checkpoints (every 1010 steps from step 1010 to step 109109, with best_ckpt_max_keep=2 top by val score), we select the checkpoint maximizing (EM+F1)/2(\mathrm{EM}+F_{1})/2 on the held-out 1,0001{,}000-query 2WikiMultiHopQA validation slice. Validation is run during training with the same retriever and inference setup as Stage II to avoid distribution shift at hand-off.

  2. 2.

    Pattern distillation. The selected best checkpoint generates trajectories on the union of training prompts; high-quality trajectories (RIDR≥0.85R_{\textsc{IDR}}\geq 0.85) are extracted and merged into a frozen ℳ0\mathcal{M}_{0} via the procedure in §C.5. We additionally log F1¯\overline{F_{1}} and RIDR¯\overline{R_{\textsc{IDR}}} per pattern for downstream diagnostic use.

  3. 3.

    Stage-II warm-start. Stage II starts from the same Stage-I best checkpoint as the policy initial state, with ℳ0\mathcal{M}_{0} loaded as read-only memory. The first Stage-II step inherits the policy’s Stage-I-end behavior, ensuring continuity.

Appendix H Prompts

We collect the three prompts that materially shape PatternBloom: the oracle scoring prompt for IDR (Stage I training), the agent system prompt at inference, and the LLM-judge rubric used for the six-axis quality ensemble in Table 17. Each prompt is reproduced verbatim from our codebase; reformatting characters (curly braces, angle brackets, hash marks) appear exactly as the model sees them. The three boxes are color-coded by deployment phase: blue for training, green for inference, plum for evaluation, so a reader can quickly locate the relevant prompt by phase.

H.1 IDR Oracle Scoring Prompt

The Information-Density Reward computes a per-graph oracle log-probability gain Δ​log⁡p𝒪​(a∗∣q,𝒢)\Delta\log p_{\mathcal{O}}(a^{*}\mid q,\mathcal{G}) on the gold answer. The oracle (Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct, served via vLLM) sees the fixed-template prefix below; the template is identical across training and inference, since shifting it would invalidate the cached log-probability baselines used for the moving-average normalizer.

The serialized graph renders each retrieved triple as head | relation | tail on its own line; the empty graph renders as the literal token (no context) so that the empty-graph baseline is well-defined. We score only the gold-answer tokens (regardless of prefix length) and average the per-token log-probabilities over the gold positions, yielding a single per-trajectory IDR signal. The trajectory IDR is then normalized by the moving average of the empty-graph baseline (Appendix B).

H.2 Agent System Prompt

The agent’s system prompt documents the three permitted actions (<query>, <graph>, <answer>) and embeds the retrieved graph patterns whenever the query signature matches a stored skeleton in ℳ\mathcal{M} above the dispatch threshold θsim=0.5\theta_{\mathrm{sim}}=0.5.

When no pattern in ℳ\mathcal{M} exceeds θsim\theta_{\mathrm{sim}} at dispatch time, the “# Retrieved reasoning patterns” block is omitted (cold-start fallback, Appendix D.1). Tables 10, 11, and 12 show this prompt instantiated on specific queries.

H.3 LLM-Judge Six-Axis Rubric

Table 17 reports six-axis quality scores averaged over three judges (Sonnet 4.6, Haiku 4.5, Gemini 2.5 Flash) on 200200 random queries drawn from the seven evaluation datasets. Each judge receives the rubric below; the response is parsed as a strict JSON object with one Likert score per axis.

The same prompt is sent to all three judges; for the Anthropic models we omit the OpenAI-specific JSON-mode parameter (response_format={"type":"json_object"}) and rely on instruction-following to produce a parseable JSON object. Judge outputs that fail JSON parsing are dropped (these account for <1%<1\% of judge calls in our run, none concentrated on PatternBloom). The reported number per axis is the mean over the three judges and over the 200200 queries.

Appendix I Discussion

I.1 Why Externalizing Graph Patterns Helps

Two observations from §4 connect the empirical gains to the paradigm shift proposed in §1. First, the IDR reward at Stage I aligns the policy gradient with the conditional information gain I⁡(𝒢;a∗∣q)I(\mathcal{G};a^{*}\mid q) rather than surface-form token overlap (Theorem 1), which prevents the verbose-but-correct graph reward-hacking mode that token-level F1 admits. Second, the Graph Pattern Memory at Stage II separates the procedural knowledge of which reasoning structure to apply from the declarative knowledge of which facts to retrieve. Since the same type-abstracted skeleton (e.g., [film]→directed_by[person]→nationality[country][\textsc{film}]\!\xrightarrow{\texttt{directed\_by}}\![\textsc{person}]\!\xrightarrow{\texttt{nationality}}\![\textsc{country}]) applies across thousands of film-director-country instances, pattern retrieval compounds with reasoning depth where content retrieval saturates, evidenced by the +10.4+10.4 EM gain on Bamboogle (4-hop) relative to HotpotQA (2-hop).

I.2 Limitations

On the empirical side, the procedural-memory mechanism transfers at the fixed Wikipedia-hyperedge substrate. Cross-domain transfer to non-Wikipedia corpora such as biomedical, legal, or financial documents lies outside the scope of the present paper and is the natural deployment-scale next benchmark.

I.3 Broader Impact

Positive.

PatternBloom reduces sample complexity for retrieval-augmented reasoning agents (Stage I IDR converges on 1414K queries) and produces an inspectable pattern library that practitioners can audit, prune, or extend. The pattern library is human-readable (typed triples), unlike opaque parametric memory in end-to-end models.

Negative.

A poorly curated GPM, for example one that absorbed adversarial trajectories without basic format and quality filters, could systematically mislead downstream users. Production systems where GPM accumulates over weeks would benefit from an LLM-judge audit before admitting new skeletons.

I.4 Future Work

Cross-domain transfer.

Type abstraction makes patterns domain-agnostic in principle, but our experiments cover only Wikipedia-grounded multi-hop QA. Whether ℳ\mathcal{M} trained on Wikipedia transfers zero-shot to medical (PubMedQA), legal, or financial QA without retraining is the natural next benchmark.

Appendix J Extended Related Work

The compact §2 introduces two adjacent research lines and our position. This appendix expands that discussion: §J.1 catalogs structured-RAG methods along five comparison axes; §J.2 catalogs RL-for-RAG methods along their reward designs; and §J.2 pins down where PatternBloom sits in the resulting design space.

J.1 Structured RAG: Method-by-Method Comparison

We organize structured-RAG methods along five axes: (i) the underlying retrieval representation; (ii) when the structure is built (build-time); (iii) what the agent receives at retrieval (retrieval unit); (iv) whether a reasoning path is exposed; and (v) how the structure is supervised (construction supervision). Table 20 summarizes the comparison.

Construction supervision.

Structure construction in prior work is supervised either by frozen-LLM heuristics (community detection, entity extraction prompts) or by GNN pre-training objectives (link prediction, node classification). None of these objectives directly optimizes “how useful is this structure for downstream multi-hop QA”. PatternBloom’s Information-Density Reward (§3.2) provides exactly this signal: the policy is rewarded for evidence graphs whose conditional information gain on the gold answer is high under a frozen oracle. Theorem 1 and Appendix E ground this reward in size-normalized conditional mutual information.

Retrieval unit and reasoning path.

Across the structured-RAG line, the retrieval unit has steadily widened from a single passage to a community summary, a hyperedge, or an adaptive structure. In every case, however, the unit returned to the agent encodes specific entity content. The agent must still infer how to traverse those fragments to reach an answer; the reasoning path lives only in the language model’s hidden state and dissolves after the query. PatternBloom’s graph patterns are typed reasoning skeletons such as (film,directed_by,person)→(person,born_in,country)(\textsc{film},\texttt{directed\_by},\textsc{person})\to(\textsc{person},\texttt{born\_in},\textsc{country}) that prescribe a directed traversal explicitly and are reusable across all instances of the same query type.

J.2 Reinforcement Learning for Agentic RAG: Reward Designs

We compare RL-for-RAG methods along three axes: their reward signal (what the policy is optimized for), their retrieval target (where the policy retrieves from), and their training-data scale. Table 21 summarizes.

Reward formulation.

Search-R1 and R1-Searcher use answer-only rewards, treating retrieval as a black-box action whose only feedback is downstream answer correctness. FrugalRAG, building on declarative LM compilation [49], augments this with a budget term that penalizes excessive search hops, addressing efficiency rather than evidence quality. Graph-R1’s entity-presence proxy is the closest prior attempt to interrogate the constructed graph (it checks whether gold-answer entities appear in the graph), but the check is binary and grants the same reward to graphs that contain the gold entity buried among 2020 other triples versus graphs that contain it among 33 relevant triples. PatternBloom’s IDR (Eq. 3) instead measures how much the constructed graph raises a frozen oracle’s likelihood of the gold answer per triple, providing a continuous, size-normalized signal that scales with reasoning depth.

Memory across episodes.

All five RL-for-RAG methods are memory-less across episodes: each query’s trajectory is generated fresh and dissolves at episode end, leaving no state that persists into the next query. Successful reasoning patterns are absorbed only into the policy’s parameters via gradient updates, where they are not directly inspectable, editable, or transferable. PatternBloom’s Graph Pattern Memory (§3.3) externalizes this procedural knowledge into a separate, human-readable, query-signature-indexed store that can be inspected, edited, and frozen for reproducibility, complementing trajectory-level techniques such as self-consistency [50] and the lifelong skill libraries explored by embodied LLM agents [51].

NeurIPS Paper Checklist

  1. 1.

    Claims

  2. Question: Do the main claims made in the abstract and introduction accurately reflect the paper’s contributions and scope?

  3. Answer: [Yes]

  4. Justification: The main claims in the abstract and Section 1 are supported by the experiments in Section 4 and the theoretical result in Appendix E.

  5. Guidelines:

    • •

      The answer [N/A] means that the abstract and introduction do not include the claims made in the paper.

    • •

      The abstract and/or introduction should clearly state the claims made, including the contributions made in the paper and important assumptions and limitations. A [No] or [N/A] answer to this question will not be perceived well by the reviewers.

    • •

      The claims made should match theoretical and experimental results, and reflect how much the results can be expected to generalize to other settings.

    • •

      It is fine to include aspirational goals as motivation as long as it is clear that these goals are not attained by the paper.

  6. 2.

    Limitations

  7. Question: Does the paper discuss the limitations of the work performed by the authors?

  8. Answer: [Yes]

  9. Justification: Limitations are discussed in Appendix I.2.

  10. Guidelines:

    • •

      The answer [N/A] means that the paper has no limitation while the answer [No] means that the paper has limitations, but those are not discussed in the paper.

    • •

      The authors are encouraged to create a separate “Limitations” section in their paper.

    • •

      The paper should point out any strong assumptions and how robust the results are to violations of these assumptions (e.g., independence assumptions, noiseless settings, model well-specification, asymptotic approximations only holding locally). The authors should reflect on how these assumptions might be violated in practice and what the implications would be.

    • •

      The authors should reflect on the scope of the claims made, e.g., if the approach was only tested on a few datasets or with a few runs. In general, empirical results often depend on implicit assumptions, which should be articulated.

    • •

      The authors should reflect on the factors that influence the performance of the approach. For example, a facial recognition algorithm may perform poorly when image resolution is low or images are taken in low lighting. Or a speech-to-text system might not be used reliably to provide closed captions for online lectures because it fails to handle technical jargon.

    • •

      The authors should discuss the computational efficiency of the proposed algorithms and how they scale with dataset size.

    • •

      If applicable, the authors should discuss possible limitations of their approach to address problems of privacy and fairness.

    • •

      While the authors might fear that complete honesty about limitations might be used by reviewers as grounds for rejection, a worse outcome might be that reviewers discover limitations that aren’t acknowledged in the paper. The authors should use their best judgment and recognize that individual actions in favor of transparency play an important role in developing norms that preserve the integrity of the community. Reviewers will be specifically instructed to not penalize honesty concerning limitations.

  11. 3.

  12. Question: For each theoretical result, does the paper provide the full set of assumptions and a complete (and correct) proof?

  14. Justification: Theorem 1 is stated and proved with full assumptions in Appendix E.

  15. Guidelines:

    • •

      The answer [N/A] means that the paper does not include theoretical results.

    • •

      All the theorems, formulas, and proofs in the paper should be numbered and cross-referenced.

    • •

      All assumptions should be clearly stated or referenced in the statement of any theorems.

    • •

      The proofs can either appear in the main paper or the supplemental material, but if they appear in the supplemental material, the authors are encouraged to provide a short proof sketch to provide intuition.

    • •

      Inversely, any informal proof provided in the core of the paper should be complemented by formal proofs provided in appendix or supplemental material.

    • •

      Theorems and Lemmas that the proof relies upon should be properly referenced.

  16. 4.

    Experimental result reproducibility

  17. Question: Does the paper fully disclose all the information needed to reproduce the main experimental results of the paper to the extent that it affects the main claims and/or conclusions of the paper (regardless of whether the code and data are provided or not)?

  18. Answer: [Yes]

  19. Justification: Implementation details, hyperparameters, and prompts are documented in Appendices B–D, G, and H.

  20. Guidelines:

    • •

      The answer [N/A] means that the paper does not include experiments.

    • •

      If the paper includes experiments, a [No] answer to this question will not be perceived well by the reviewers: Making the paper reproducible is important, regardless of whether the code and data are provided or not.

    • •

      If the contribution is a dataset and/or model, the authors should describe the steps taken to make their results reproducible or verifiable.

    • •

      Depending on the contribution, reproducibility can be accomplished in various ways. For example, if the contribution is a novel architecture, describing the architecture fully might suffice, or if the contribution is a specific model and empirical evaluation, it may be necessary to either make it possible for others to replicate the model with the same dataset, or provide access to the model. In general. releasing code and data is often one good way to accomplish this, but reproducibility can also be provided via detailed instructions for how to replicate the results, access to a hosted model (e.g., in the case of a large language model), releasing of a model checkpoint, or other means that are appropriate to the research performed.

    • •

      While NeurIPS does not require releasing code, the conference does require all submissions to provide some reasonable avenue for reproducibility, which may depend on the nature of the contribution. For example

      1. (a)

        If the contribution is primarily a new algorithm, the paper should make it clear how to reproduce that algorithm.

      2. (b)

        If the contribution is primarily a new model architecture, the paper should describe the architecture clearly and fully.

      3. (c)

        If the contribution is a new model (e.g., a large language model), then there should either be a way to access this model for reproducing the results or a way to reproduce the model (e.g., with an open-source dataset or instructions for how to construct the dataset).

      4. (d)

        We recognize that reproducibility may be tricky in some cases, in which case authors are welcome to describe the particular way they provide for reproducibility. In the case of closed-source models, it may be that access to the model is limited in some way (e.g., to registered users), but it should be possible for other researchers to have some path to reproducing or verifying the results.

      Depending on the country in which research is conducted, IRB approval (or equivalent) may be required for any human subjects research. If you obtained IRB approval, you should clearly state this in the paper.

    • •

      We recognize that the procedures for this may vary significantly between institutions and locations, and we expect authors to adhere to the NeurIPS Code of Ethics and the guidelines for their institution.

    • •

      For initial submissions, do not include any information that would break anonymity (if applicable), such as the institution conducting the review.

  76. 16.

    Declaration of LLM usage

  77. Question: Does the paper describe the usage of LLMs if it is an important, original, or non-standard component of the core methods in this research? Note that if the LLM is used only for writing, editing, or formatting purposes and does not impact the core methodology, scientific rigor, or originality of the research, declaration is not required.

    • •

      The answer [N/A] means that the core method development in this research does not involve LLMs as any important, original, or non-standard components.
